pass2.notificationLine: Reading flips to augmentation: prime-age employment share flat at 80.4%, layoffs low
pass2.publishedNote:
The reading flips to augmentation this month, and it rests on the absence of deterioration rather than on evidence that AI is making workers more valuable. Nothing here shows augmentation working. What it shows is that the places where displacement would have to appear — people losing work and not finding new work — still do not show it, and that the one AI-specific measure that moved, moved slightly the right way. Confidence is low.

What changed: jobs in AI-exposed industries improved a little relative to the rest of the economy. Exposed industries are still shrinking, at 1.19% a year, while control industries add jobs at 1.16% — but the exposed side shrank less than it did last month. Productivity for the whole economy slowed to 2.2% growth from 2.9%. Everything else is unchanged, including the employment panel the reading actually turns on.

That panel is the share of 25-to-54-year-olds with a job: 80.4%, exactly where it was a year ago and about 0.45 points above its 2019 level. Layoffs are running at 1.1% of employment a month, low and lower than a year ago. Economy-wide, people who change employers are still landing at a pay premium over people who stay, 4.4% against 3.6%. If a category of work were being removed, this is where it would show, and it does not.

Against that, the number that cuts hardest: the share of national income going to workers rather than capital is 51.0%, the lowest in the record, down four quarters running and falling at roughly seven times its forty-year drift. Two things stop it from deciding the question, and neither is a dismissal. It covers every industry, so it cannot separate AI-exposed work from anything else — unlike the exposed-industry figures above, which cover a different and much smaller group of workers. And ordinary recessions have produced faster falls, 2.2 points in 2009. It is also the oldest figure here, from March, predating the July labour data. It stays on the watch list.

Three more things sit badly with the verdict. First, the standard benign explanation for exposed-industry weakness — that these industries over-hired in 2021-22 and have been unwinding since — no longer covers the present. We are four years past the hiring peak, an unwind should be closing, and instead exposed industries are contracting outright while job postings for knowledge work sit 23% below their February 2020 level with no recovery, against hands-on postings 5% above theirs. That residual is what keeps a displacement story alive.

Second, the market is frozen rather than healthy. Hiring is running at 3.4% of employment a month, low historically, and the improvement in the balance between hiring and quitting came from fewer people quitting, not more people being hired. Low layoffs plus low hiring means incumbents keep their jobs and the cost falls on people trying to get in — which is what an early, slow AI displacement would look like, and also what a high-rate, high-uncertainty economy looks like. This data cannot tell them apart.

Third, the flat employment share is doing less work than it appears. Prime-age employment actually fell over the year; the share held steady because the prime-age population fell too. That is a labour-supply story, most likely immigration, not a job-destruction story — but it is not the clean hold it looks like. And the gap between broad underemployment and headline unemployment, at 3.8 points and up 0.2 over the year, is the most deteriorated single reading on the board, though its last three months moved the other way.

One number I am deliberately not using: pay in exposed industries is growing 4.22% a year against 3.21% elsewhere, which looks like augmentation. But employment there is falling, and when entry-level hiring stops the remaining workforce skews senior and the average rises without anyone getting a raise. A real pay story and a bookkeeping artefact predict the same figure, so it counts for nothing in either direction.

What to watch: the prime-age employment chart. If its 12-month change turns down while control industries keep adding jobs, people leaving exposed work are not being reabsorbed, and this reading was wrong.
pass2.fullAnalysis:
The reading this month is augmentation, and it has flipped from displacement. Before anything else: this is not a finding that AI is visibly making workers more valuable. It is a finding that the places where displacement would have to show up — people losing work and not finding new work — still do not show it, while the one AI-specific measure that moved, moved slightly the right way. Confidence is low. The honest description is "displacement has not appeared in the absorption data," not "augmentation is demonstrably working."

What moved since last month

Four numbers changed. Jobs in AI-exposed industries relative to control industries improved slightly: exposed industries are shrinking at 1.19% a year while control industries add jobs at 1.16% a year, so the gap between them is 2.35 percentage points, narrower than the 2.54 points a month ago. Naming the sides matters here: the improvement came from the exposed side shrinking a little less, not from control racing ahead. Productivity for the whole economy fell to 2.2% growth a year from 2.9%. Pay growth in exposed industries relative to control narrowed a touch, to 1.00 points from 1.11. And a benchmark of AI model quality ticked up fractionally.

Everything else on the board is unchanged from last month, including the panel the reading actually rests on.

Why the reading is augmentation

The decisive measure is the share of 25-to-54-year-olds who have a job. It is 80.4%, unchanged from a year ago, and about 0.45 points above where it sat in 2019 before the pandemic. If AI were pushing people out of exposed work faster than the rest of the economy could take them in, this is the number that would sag, and it has not.

Around it, the layoff rate is 1.1% of employment per month, low by historical standards and lower than a year ago. Employers are not shedding people. The share of the unemployed who have been out of work more than six months is 25.5%, up 0.6 points over the year — rising, but only barely, which means people who lose jobs are still being caught roughly as fast as before. Economy-wide, people who change employers are still landing at a pay premium over people who stay put, 4.4% against 3.6%, and that premium has been recovering over recent readings. Job-changers getting paid more is what reallocation with decent landings looks like; it is not what an economy looks like when a category of work is being removed.

On the AI-specific side, the gap between online job postings for knowledge work and postings for hands-on work narrowed by 2.6 points over six months.

The cyclical alternative, and why it does not fully clear

The obvious rival explanation for shrinking employment in information, professional services and finance is not AI at all — it is interest rates. The 10-year yield is 2.4% above expected inflation, which is restrictive. If that were the whole story, though, you would expect the control industries to be struggling too, and construction, the most rate-sensitive industry there is, sits inside the control group and is not dragging it negative; control industries are still adding jobs. The yield curve is not inverted. So the weakness is specific to the exposed industries rather than general.

That test is not clean, and I want to be precise about where it fails. Real estate and insurance sit inside the exposed group and are themselves rate-sensitive. Temporary help sits inside professional and business services, and temp help turns down first in any slowdown regardless of cause. Professional services also carries heavy federal contracting exposure. A rate squeeze plus a contracting squeeze plus a temp-help unwind could produce a 1.19% contraction with no AI in it at all. Nothing in this data separates those from an AI effect.

The 2021-22 over-hiring story, and the residual it leaves

The standard benign explanation for the exposed-industry gap is that these industries hired far too many people in 2021 and 2022 and have been giving those jobs back ever since. That explains the deepest part of the trough well — the widest the gap ever got was in late 2023, which was also when the writers' and actors' strikes shut down large parts of the information sector.

It explains the present much less well. We are more than four years past the hiring peak. An unwind should be finished, or at least still closing. Instead exposed industries are not merely growing more slowly than the rest of the economy, they are contracting outright, and job postings for knowledge work sit 23% below where they were in February 2020 with no recovery, while postings for hands-on work sit 5% above theirs. That residual — the part the hiring correction does not account for — is what keeps a displacement story alive, and it is the main reason confidence here is low rather than moderate.

The postings improvement has a hole in it. The 2.6-point narrowing over six months is a change in the gap, and I cannot see from this data which side produced it. Knowledge-work postings recovering and hands-on postings weakening would both narrow the gap by the same amount, and only one of those is good news. I am not treating that narrowing as strong support.

The frozen market

The hiring rate is 3.4% of employment a month and the quit rate is 2.0%. The gap between hiring and quitting improved over the year, but it improved because quitting fell, not because hiring rose. Hiring at 3.4% is low by historical standards. Layoffs low plus hiring low is a frozen market rather than a shedding one: incumbents keep their jobs, and the cost falls on people trying to get in.

That shape is genuinely ambiguous. It is exactly what a slow AI displacement would look like in its early years, where nobody is fired but nobody is hired either. It is also exactly what a restrictive-rates, high-uncertainty economy produces. I cannot tell them apart, and I say so rather than counting the improvement as strength.

The number that cuts hardest against this reading

The share of national income going to workers rather than to capital is 51.0%. That is below the previous record low in the data, set in December 2025. It has fallen four quarters running, down about 1.0 point over the year, which is roughly seven times the pace of the slow secular decline that has run for forty years and puts this among the fastest declines on record.

NOTIFICATION: Reading flips to augmentation: prime-age employment share flat at 80.4%, layoffs low
TAGLINE: Flipped on absent deterioration
FULL_ANALYSIS:
The reading this month is augmentation, and it has flipped from displacement. Before anything else: this is not a finding that AI is visibly making workers more valuable. It is a finding that the places where displacement would have to show up — people losing work and not finding new work — still do not show it, while the one AI-specific measure that moved, moved slightly the right way. Confidence is low. The honest description is "displacement has not appeared in the absorption data," not "augmentation is demonstrably working."

What moved since last month

Four numbers changed. Jobs in AI-exposed industries relative to control industries improved slightly: exposed industries are shrinking at 1.19% a year while control industries add jobs at 1.16% a year, so the gap between them is 2.35 percentage points, narrower than the 2.54 points a month ago. Naming the sides matters here: the improvement came from the exposed side shrinking a little less, not from control racing ahead. Productivity for the whole economy fell to 2.2% growth a year from 2.9%. Pay growth in exposed industries relative to control narrowed a touch, to 1.00 points from 1.11. And a benchmark of AI model quality ticked up fractionally.

Everything else on the board is unchanged from last month, including the panel the reading actually rests on.

Why the reading is augmentation

The decisive measure is the share of 25-to-54-year-olds who have a job. It is 80.4%, unchanged from a year ago, and about 0.45 points above where it sat in 2019 before the pandemic. If AI were pushing people out of exposed work faster than the rest of the economy could take them in, this is the number that would sag, and it has not.

Around it, the layoff rate is 1.1% of employment per month, low by historical standards and lower than a year ago. Employers are not shedding people. The share of the unemployed who have been out of work more than six months is 25.5%, up 0.6 points over the year — rising, but only barely, which means people who lose jobs are still being caught roughly as fast as before. Economy-wide, people who change employers are still landing at a pay premium over people who stay put, 4.4% against 3.6%, and that premium has been recovering over recent readings. Job-changers getting paid more is what reallocation with decent landings looks like; it is not what an economy looks like when a category of work is being removed.

On the AI-specific side, the gap between online job postings for knowledge work and postings for hands-on work narrowed by 2.6 points over six months.

The obvious rival explanation for shrinking employment in information, professional services and finance is not AI at all — it is interest rates. That test is not clean, and I want to be precise about where it fails. Real estate and insurance sit inside the exposed group and are themselves rate-sensitive. The standard benign explanation for the exposed-industry gap is that these industries hired far too many people in 2021 and 2022 and have been giving those jobs back ever since. runs.computedDissent: The analyst read AUGMENTATION from the panels without being shown either mechanical reading, and the four-corner grid places this month at DISPLACEMENT (gap wide and holding, aggregate deteriorating). Recorded, not resolved: these are different routes through the same data, and neither one overrules the other. The grid in particular turns on a single economy-wide series sitting near zero, so a month's disagreement with it is ordinary rather than a mark against either reading.

pass1.confidenceBasis: Corroborating — reabsorption (economy-wide, 2026-07: headline prime-age employment share 12-month change 0.0 at 0.8σ, below its own attention line, level 0.45pt above 2019; layoffs rate 1.1 and falling, -0.34σ; long-term-unemployed share up only 0.6pt, 0.31σ), job_postings_spread (2026-07: spread narrowed 2.6 points over six months, -1.17σ against its own contaminated history), individual_wage_growth (economy-wide, 2026-06: switcher premium 0.8, inside its 2010s range and recovering). Failing to corroborate or cutting against — exposed_vs_control_jobs (2026-07: exposed employment outright -1.19% y/y against control +1.16%, 1.82σ past the attention line, and the attribution z has re-widened from 0.96 in 2025-11 to 1.82 now while AI adoption rose 17.3→21.5%), reabsorption's own fast horizon (3-month prime-age change -0.3 at 1.95σ, disagreeing with the headline it sits under) and the U-6 minus U-3 gap (+0.2pt, 1.81σ), worker_share_of_income (51.0, a record low in a series back to 1947, 4-quarter change -1.0, fastest decile — but economy-wide and 5 months stale). Unmet doubt: the leading edge inside my own key panel points the other way, and three of the four reabsorption readouts I lean on are the same household survey, so their agreement is nearer one measurement than three; JOLTS layoffs is the one genuinely independent source and it agrees with me.

falsifier.unit: percentage points of the 25-54 population, change over 12 months

pass1.falsifierPlain: The prime-age employment share moves first — if its 12-month change falls to -0.6 points or worse while control industries are still adding jobs at 0.8% a year or better, the outflow from AI-exposed work is no longer landing and this reading is wrong.
pass1.reasoningLog:
**0. What this run is, and how quiet it is**

Run date 2026-08-08; the previous run was 2026-08-07, one day earlier, on the same data month (2026-07). The change list names exactly one moving panel: the 10y-2y spread, 0.4 → 0.5. Everything else is byte-identical to yesterday. So before anything else: the panels have not moved. Whatever I say here is a re-reading of a static picture, not a response to news in the series, and that alone caps confidence. I am told not to see the previous verdict and I have not; I am reasoning from the panels.

I state up front, as required: **my support rests mainly on the absence of deterioration, not on positive evidence of augmentation.** I am reading "workers are moving rather than being removed," not "AI is making exposed workers more valuable." The one panel that would carry the positive claim — exposed pay running 1.0 point ahead of control — is disqualified from carrying it by its own composition artifact (below), and the economy-wide productivity check returned no break. So this is a directional call on the reallocation-vs-removal axis, filed on the augmentation side because the removal signature is absent, and it is LOW for exactly that reason.

**1. exposed_vs_control_jobs (as_of 2026-07, 1 month old) — ATTRIBUTION**

Naming the moving side rather than the gap: exposed industries (information, professional/business, financial) are at **-1.19% year-over-year — an outright contraction**. Control industries (construction, leisure/hospitality, education/health) are at **+1.16%**. The differential is -2.35, prior month -2.57.

Deviation: 1.82σ against the fixed 2010-01..2019-12 window, 0.59σ against full history. The divergence note flags the classic pattern — the reading looks tamer against a window that has swallowed 2023-2026 — so I reason from the pre-2020 figure, 1.82σ. That is past the attention line of 1 and short of the alarm line of 2. The registered trigger is -2.48; last month's -2.57 was past it and this month's -2.35 is not. The panel effectively de-escalated by one notch this month.

Contemporaneous macro test, which is the one that counts: if this were a general downturn, the control leg would be weak too. It is not — control is adding jobs at 1.16% a year, and control postings (below) sit 5.3% *above* their own pre-pandemic level. Note especially that **construction, the most interest-rate-sensitive industry in the economy, sits in the control leg**, and the control leg is healthy while the real 10-year yield is 2.4%. That is the strongest single argument against reading the exposed-side weakness as a pure rate story — though it does not fully clear rates, because the exposed leg carries real estate and insurance, which are rate-sensitive in a different way (asset values and transaction volumes, not construction employment). I cannot separate that from this payload.

Two other non-AI candidates live inside the exposed leg and I want them on the record even though nothing here lets me test either: (a) the 2023 writers'/actors' strikes sit inside the months this differential was widest — the joint table's attribution_z peaks at 5.66 in 2023-11, exactly there, so the historical extreme of this series is partly a labour dispute in motion pictures, with no AI in it; (b) professional and business services contains temporary help and federal contracting, both of which turn early and hard for reasons unrelated to AI. Neither is a series I can point to in this payload, so neither reaches the bar for CONFOUNDED. They are reasons to hold the attribution loosely.

Revision hazard, from the panel's own methodology note: the two most recent CES months are preliminary, the birth-death model misses turning points in both directions, and annual benchmarking has recently run to hundreds of thousands of jobs. So the -1.19/+1.16 pair, and particularly the one-month narrowing from -2.57 to -2.35, is the least reliable part of the series. I am not treating this month's narrowing as a finding; I am treating the four-month flat stretch around -2.3 to -2.6 as the finding.

**The binding weighting rule on this panel is that a widening gap is not displacement.** The mechanics are worked out in the artifact and they are right: 100 jobs destroyed in information and 100 workers hired in health care produces the maximally negative reading here with nobody left behind. So this panel establishes that something is specific to AI-exposed work, and I accept that it does. It cannot establish that work was destroyed.

**Inversion of this panel (it is an attribution panel that cuts against my verdict, so the inversion runs the other way — what is the strongest reading under which it supports ME?):** the gap is *parked, not widening*, and it has fallen back inside its trigger. Over the last four readings it is roughly flat. Against the 2023 peak of 5.66σ it is now 1.82σ — a third as extreme. A divergence that peaked in 2023 and has converged since, while AI capability and adoption both rose steadily, is a poor fit for an AI-driven story and a good fit for the post-ZIRP white-collar retrenchment plus a strike, both of which are dated events unwinding.

**Against my own reading, honestly:** that convergence story breaks if you look at the window over which I actually have an adoption series. Attribution_z bottomed at 0.96 in 2025-11 and has re-widened to 1.84, 1.91, 1.90, 1.94, 2.14, 2.11, 1.82 across 2026-01 through 2026-07, while firm AI adoption rose 17.3 → 21.5%. So over the only nine months where I can put the two series side by side, **the exposed-vs-control gap re-widened as adoption rose.** That is a correlation between two aggregates with no firm-level linkage — the Census survey asks whether a tool is present, not whether any use case made a role redundant, and nothing connects one firm's "yes" to that same firm's headcount — so it licenses no mechanism. But it is the single strongest thing in this payload pointing at displacement, it is why my confidence is LOW rather than MEDIUM, and it is why my overturn condition is set on absorption rather than on something safe.

**2. reabsorption (as_of 2026-07 for household components, 2026-06 for JOLTS) — the panel that decides**

Population: economy-wide throughout. None of this is an exposed-industry figure and I am not treating it as one.

*Headline (binding).* Prime-age employment share 80.4%, **12-month change 0.0**, deviation 0.8σ against the fixed pre-2020 window — below the attention line. Level 0.45 points above its 2019 reference. The two baselines agree here (divergence 0.08), so this reading does not depend on window choice. On the measure the panel designates as placing the axis, absorption is holding.

The decomposition is unusable for magnitudes and says so: both the employed and population legs step through the January Census control re-basing (roughly +1.7m and -1.0m on the employed leg at Jan-2025 and Jan-2026 respectively, against a normal month of 100-200k), so any 12-month change spans a break on both sides. The ratio re-bases numerator and denominator together and is the reliable object. I take only the direction check from it and quote none of the level changes. I also note the payload's own warning: the -779k employed figure here is CPS, ages 25-54, twelve months, and the -23k payroll figure in the news package is CES, all ages, one month. Three things differ at once. They are not netted and neither refutes the other.

*Fast horizon (context only, and the main threat to my verdict).* The 3-month change is **-0.3, at 1.95σ against the clean pre-2020 window** — just short of the alarm line, and it disagrees with the headline. The panel is explicit that this is a hypothesis about a turn rather than a finding, and that a 3-month move on a noisy monthly series must not move a verdict by itself. I am citing the 12-month horizon for the verdict and flagging the 3-month as the reason I am at LOW and the reason my overturn sits on this exact field. If the fast horizon is the truth arriving early, I am wrong within a quarter, which is precisely the outcome the overturn machinery exists to record.

*Layoffs and hiring, read as a pair as the panel demands.* Layoffs and discharges 1.1, 12-month change -0.1, deviation -0.34σ (away from displacement) and the 3-month at -0.94σ. Hires 3.4, quits 2.0, net 1.4, 12-month change +0.1, deviation -0.90σ (away from displacement). Read together per the panel's rule: layoffs at or below norm alongside unspectacular hiring is a **FROZEN market, not a cyclical contraction**. Firms are not shedding incumbents; they are not replacing exits. That distinction matters enormously here, because it tells me the -1.19% in exposed industries is very likely attrition and hiring freeze rather than discharge — and *that is compatible with both my verdict and the opposite one*, which I take up in the inversion.

Naming the moving side on hires-minus-quits, as required: the net rose 0.1 over twelve months, but the payload gives me only current levels (3.4 and 2.0) and the net's change, not each side's year-ago level. **I cannot tell whether the net improved because hiring picked up or because quitting fell further.** A rising hires-minus-quits driven by collapsing quits is workers afraid to move, not a market absorbing people, and it would read as improvement on this readout. That is an unresolved question inside a panel I am leaning on, and it weakens the readout materially. I am not going to pretend otherwise.

*Long-term unemployed share.* 25.5%, +0.6 points over twelve months, 0.31σ — essentially nothing against a baseline whose standard deviation is 5.2 points. Exits are still being caught reasonably quickly. This is the readout that would light up first if people who left exposed work were failing to land, and it has not.

*Underemployment gap (U-6 minus U-3).* 3.8, +0.2 over twelve months, **1.81σ against the fixed window**, though the 3-month change is -0.1 (improving) and sits at 0.0σ. This is the displacement-side readout on this panel and I take it seriously as the "landing badly" channel. One caveat I want on the record, from the panel's own construction: the baseline for 12-month *changes* here is drawn from 2010-2019, a decade of continuously narrowing underemployment (mean change -0.35 per year). Against a decade that improved every year, a +0.2 year scores as 1.8σ of deterioration when in level terms it is a move from 3.6 to 3.8. The panel explicitly acknowledged this problem for *levels* and fixed it for the headline by using a 2019 reference point instead; it did not apply the same fix to the change baselines on the secondaries. So I read the 1.81σ as real but inflated by the baseline decade's direction, and I note the fast horizon is going the other way.

*Vintage inside the panel.* Household series to 2026-07, JOLTS to 2026-06. One month, stated, immaterial — but it means a very recent turn would appear in the headline before it appeared in layoffs and hiring, and the headline's fast horizon is the thing that is wobbling. Worth holding.

*Joint position.* 34 of 42 observation months sit outside the 2σ baseline joint range, against 11 of 120 baseline months. That is a genuine finding about the period as a whole: this combination of readings is unusual against the 2010s. But it is dominated by 2023-2024, when attribution_z ran 3-5 with the strikes inside it, and the most recent month (2026-07: z 1.82, employment change 0.0) is back *inside* the baseline range. Months 2026-04, -05 and -06 were outside. It flickers. Also noted, per the panel's instruction: 2025-10 is absent from the table entirely, so any slope drawn across that point is drawn across more than a month.

**Inversion of the reabsorption panel — the best version of the case that these same numbers support DISPLACEMENT:**

- A flat aggregate employment ratio is exactly what *successful reabsorption into worse work* looks like, and the U-6 gap widening 1.81σ is what that would leave behind. Perfect displacement with everyone re-employed part-time or below their skill produces a flat headline and a widening U-6. My headline reading cannot distinguish that from health, and the one readout designed to catch it is the one at 1.8σ.
- The ratio is restricted to ages 25-54 *on purpose*, which is the right call for retirements but blinds it to a displacement episode that falls on entrants. And the frozen-market signature I just described — low layoffs, unreplaced exits — is precisely the shape that pushes the whole burden onto people trying to get in. Nobody aged 22-24 is in this panel. If AI is eating entry-level knowledge work, this dashboard would show me a flat prime-age ratio, a low layoff rate, and a depressed exposed-postings index, which is exactly what it is showing me. **I regard this as the strongest argument against my verdict and I do not have a panel that answers it.** It is a reason for LOW, and if the payload ever gains a 20-24 employment series it may reverse this reading outright.
- Low and falling layoffs is not evidence against displacement at all. AI-driven job removal via attrition and hiring freeze never touches JTSLDR. So my second-best corroborating readout only rules out the cyclical-shedding variety of displacement, not the variety this dashboard exists to detect.
- The 3-month headline change at 1.95σ can be read as the turn already beginning, with the 12-month window not yet able to show it.

I have weighed all four. What holds me on the augmentation side is that the removal signature requires people to *stop landing*, and the two readouts that measure landing directly — long-term unemployed share (0.31σ) and the layoff rate (-0.34σ) — are both quiet, and the second of those comes from JOLTS, a genuinely different instrument from the household survey that produces the other three. If people were being removed at the scale implied by -1.19% across three large sectors for a year, I would expect the long-term unemployed share to have moved more than 0.6 points.

**3. job_postings_spread (as_of 2026-07) — ATTRIBUTION, earliest-moving**

Naming both sides against their own baselines, as required, before any spread: **exposed knowledge-work postings sit at 76.9, i.e. 23.1% below their own February 2020 level. Control hands-on postings sit at 105.3, 5.3% above theirs.** That is a standing, severe depression in advertised knowledge-work demand alongside healthy hands-on demand. It is strong attribution — a general contraction pulls both legs down and this has not — and it is the second instrument, on a different cut (occupation, not industry) and from a different source (Indeed, not BLS), agreeing that the weakness is specific to knowledge work. I weight the occupational cut *above* the industry cut on exposure, since a janitor in the information sector is not exposed and a data analyst in manufacturing is.

The panel's binding weighting rule is to read the change, not the level, because the spread opened in 2022 — before current tools diffused into hiring, and coincident with the tightening cycle rather than with any model release. So: **spread_change_over_6_months = +2.6**, i.e. narrowing. Against its own (contaminated, 2023-onward) history the current -28.4 is -1.17σ, on the away-from-displacement side of a mean of -33.5. The exposed side has not been getting worse over six months.

The panel also states plainly what it is not: hands-on strength is a fact about hands-on work and says nothing about whether exposed workers are being made more valuable; augmentation on this panel would be knowledge-work postings recovering *toward their own baseline*. At 76.9 they have not recovered. So this panel gives me "not deteriorating," not "improving," and certainly not augmentation.

**Inversion:** the spread can narrow because exposed postings recovered *or because control postings fell*, and the payload gives me each side's level but not each side's six-month change — **so I cannot name the moving side on the thing I am actually citing.** If the narrowing came from control weakening, that is a deteriorating economy misread as an exposed-side recovery, and it would support the opposite verdict. Second inversion: 2.6 points off a -33.5 average is small relative to the series' 4.37 standard deviation, so it may be noise. Third: postings lead employment, and a leading indicator that has been sitting 23% below baseline for years is a standing prediction of continued weakness in exposed hiring regardless of which way the last six months wobbled. I accept all three. This panel is the third leg of my reading and the weakest of the three.

**4. exposed_vs_control_wages (as_of 2026-07) — cited, NOT leaned on**

Exposed pay +4.22% y/y, control +3.21%, differential +1.00 (prior 0.93), deviation -0.60σ (away from displacement), 24 consecutive readings inside its 2010s range. Exposed workers' average pay is pulling ahead, which on its face is the augmentation signature.

**I am not leaning on it, and here is why in my own words.** The panel's own field says exposed employment is falling at -1.19%. This is an average over a group whose membership is changing while the group shrinks. If entry-level hiring in exposed industries has stopped — which is exactly what the frozen-market reading of the JOLTS pair and the -23% exposed postings index both imply — then the juniors have left the denominator and the average rises with nobody receiving a raise. A genuine pay story and the composition story predict the identical observation, and nothing in this payload separates them. The control leg has the mirror problem in the opposite direction: it contains leisure and hospitality, low-wage and growing, which drags the control average down mechanically. So both legs of this differential are moving for reasons that have nothing to do with what any individual is paid.

The designated cross-check, individual_wage_growth, is economy-wide and cannot be cut to exposed industries, so it cannot resolve this. It can only tell me the aggregate reading is not being contradicted, and it isn't: stayers 3.6%, switchers 4.4%, premium 0.8, inside its pre-2020 range (mean 0.58, sd 0.41), deviation -0.54σ, recovering over the last four readings. Composition cannot move that series because it follows the same people twelve months apart. So: economy-wide, people who change jobs are still getting paid more for it, at a normal premium. That is the cleanest available evidence that movers are landing *well* — and "landing well" is the part the reabsorption panel cannot see.

**Inversion of individual_wage_growth:** the switcher premium is itself a selection statistic, as the panel says — if the weaker candidates lose the ability to move at all, the median switcher's gain rises while the marginal worker's outcome collapses. It is a *median*, so a collapse concentrated in a minority of workers is precisely the shape it would miss, and an early displacement episode is exactly that shape. It is economy-wide, so it can never be evidence about AI-exposed work. It is CPS-based through a period of degraded response rates, with October 2025 missing outright at source, and it is 2 months old. I accept all of that: it is a corroborating panel of modest weight, not a pillar.

**5. labor_productivity (as_of 2026-06) — GAINS_TEST, economy-wide**

2.2%, down from 2.9%. Above the pre-2020 mean of 1.27 by 0.83σ, but **below the panel's 2.7-3.4 "internet-boom" band and far below the 3.4-for-two-quarters break rule. One reading below the band.** So: no productivity break. The gains AI is supposed to deliver are not visible in the aggregate at the scale that would make the augmentation story affirmative.

**Inversion, and it is sharp:** if productivity gains *were* AI-driven and concentrated in exposed industries while exposed hours fell -1.19%, then output-per-hour rising is the *displacement* arithmetic — the same output from fewer hours — not the augmentation one. An economy-wide aggregate cannot tell those apart, and it is heavily revised besides. So this panel does not support my verdict; it returns "no break," which is consistent with augmentation being too new to register, with there being no gains, and with gains arriving through headcount reduction. I count it as a check that failed to find positive evidence for my side, and I say so rather than dressing 0.83σ above a 2010s mean up as an AI dividend.

**6. worker_share_of_income (as_of 2026-03, 5 months old) — DESCRIPTIVE, no vote, economy-wide**

51.0% of gross domestic income, which is **below the previous full-history low of 51.19 (2025-12) in a series running back to 1947**. Four consecutive quarterly declines. 4-quarter change -1.0, in the fastest 10% of declines on record. One-year drift -0.96/yr against a 40-year pace of -0.13/yr — roughly seven times the secular rate.

This panel votes on nothing and I am not putting it in the load-bearing list, but I am not going to leave a genuine finding out either: a record low, falling in its fastest decile, is worth saying out loud. The weakness I am accepting in order to say it: it is economy-wide, so it cannot attribute anything to AI-exposed work; the share has fallen for forty years for causes predating AI; the panel's own note points out that ordinary recessions produced faster falls (-2.18 in 2009, -1.59 in 2010), so "falling fast" is normally a business-cycle statement. What makes this one non-trivial is that **we are not in a recession** — unemployment 4.1%, payrolls roughly flat, yield curve positive at +0.5 — and a fastest-decile fall in labour share outside a recession is not the usual pattern. It is 5 months old, a gap of four months against the 2026-07 panels, which is the one comparison in this analysis that exceeds a quarter, and I flag it: **the main evidence arguing against my verdict on this axis is older than the evidence supporting it**, so it cannot yet reflect any recent turn in either direction. If Q2 lands at 50.x with the labour market still calm, that hardens the displacement case considerably.

**7. ai_adoption (as_of 2026-07) — deployment context**

21.5% of firms, up from 20.6, and up steadily from 17.3% in 2025-11. Size gradient: 20.8% at 1-4 employees against 36.8% at 250+, ratio 1.77, so worker exposure is meaningfully higher than the firm-count headline (no employment weights are published and I am not going to invent a worker-weighted percentage).

What I take from it: deployment is real and rising, which removes the objection that an AI explanation is unavailable. What I do not take from it: any evidence that anyone lost work. The survey asks whether a tool is present in any business function, not whether a use case made a role redundant, and there is no firm-level linkage — nothing connects a given firm's "yes" to that firm's hiring freeze. It is self-reported by firms with a reason to look forward-leaning, over a respondent panel that rotates between collections, so month-to-month moves can be a change in who answered. A rise here removes an objection; it supplies no reason.

The one thing I did do with it is the timing check in section 1: adoption rose 17.3 → 21.5% over the same nine months in which the attribution z re-widened from 0.96 to 1.82. Two aggregates moving together, no mechanism, but I logged it because it cuts against me.

**8. Panels that contribute nothing, read anyway**

*ai_capability_metr* (2026-04): frontier 80% horizon 186 minutes. The task suite is clean, self-contained, auto-scorable software and cyber problems with contractor baselines and no prior context; horizons past ~960 minutes are beyond what it can score. The dashboard's own 2400-minute "working week" bar sits 2.5x past the instrument ceiling, and the naive 2027-10 crossing is one of four fits that disagree materially. None of this is an event in anyone's employment. Noted, counted in nothing.

*ai_capability_gdpval_ratings* (2026-08): Claude Opus 5 at 1846 Elo, 104 points clear of the next model. Model-versus-model with no human in the pool, so levels mean nothing and only differences carry information. Which lab leads is not a step in any chain that ends in a job.

*ai_capability_vs_human_experts* (2025-12, 8 months stale): 70.9% wins-plus-ties, and the parity caveat matters — true parity is wins-only, where the figure is 49.7%, and the number is OpenAI reporting on OpenAI's own benchmark. Nothing published since 2025-12; the gap is an instrument gap, not a capability statement. This is the most persuasive-looking capability panel because there is a human on the other side, which is the reason to handle it carefully rather than a reason to weight it. Clearing an expert on a benchmark task is not an employer deciding to stop paying that expert.

*ai_use_automation_vs_augmentation* (2025-09, 11 months stale): 43.1/56.9, essentially unmoved across three releases. It is one vendor's conversations over a user base that changes between releases, and it is the stalest panel here while measuring the fastest-moving thing on the dashboard — it predates every labor month I am reading by most of a year. The only thing worth saying is that the split was stable over the releases that exist. It plays no part in the verdict.

*macro_regime* (2026-08): real 10-year 2.4%, 10y-2y +0.5 (up from 0.4, the only change since the last run), expected inflation 2.3%, **curve not inverted**. This can name a competing cause; it cannot clear one, because it prices expectations rather than history. What I use it for: the bond market is not pricing an ordinary recession, so the cyclical hypothesis does not get free corroboration here — but I explicitly do not use the non-inverted curve to exculpate the exposed-side weakness already sitting in the CES and Indeed data. The contemporaneous test is the one I ran, in section 1, on the control legs, and it came back saying the weakness is not general.

**9. News package**

*BLS Employment Situation, through 2026-07:* nonfarm payrolls 158,858k, **-23k on the month**; unemployment 4.1%. This is economy-wide, all ages, establishment survey, one month. It is soft, and it fits the frozen-market reading (low layoffs, unreplaced exits) better than either a boom or a shedding contraction. It does not distinguish exposed from control, so it cannot move an attribution reading, and one preliminary month of CES is the least reliable object on offer. It does *not* refute the flat prime-age employment ratio and I have not netted the two: different survey, different age range, different horizon. Revisions to prior months are legitimate veto material and I would watch them, but none are reported here.

*AP wire, Iran war / energy / mortgages / job openings:* a war can move energy prices, inflation expectations and hiring. Two reasons it does not move this verdict. First, timing — it is too recent to be inside the June and July industry data at any scale, and it cannot explain a knowledge-work postings deficit that has been sitting at 20-30% since 2022. Second, shape — an energy and confidence shock hits consumer-facing, transport and energy-intensive work, most of which is in my control leg, and the control leg is the healthy one. If a war shock were driving this, the divergence would run the other way. The mortgage/rates thread is more interesting, because it is a live confounder for the real-estate and insurance component of the exposed leg, and real yields at 2.4% are not accommodative. What limits it is that the most rate-sensitive industry in the economy, construction, sits in the *control* leg and is growing. So rates can explain part of the exposed leg and cannot explain the control leg's health. Noted, not sufficient for CONFOUNDED, because I cannot point to a series in this payload that isolates it.

*NY Fed Liberty Street, "AI's Impact on Labor and Hiring":* a hypothesis generator, and I have only the title. Whatever it concludes is published analysis about some period, not a measurement of this quarter, and I will not substitute a remembered or inferred finding for the series in front of me. What I did instead was ask what such a piece would predict and test it here: if employers are cutting because of AI, the discharge rate should be rising and it is falling (1.1, -0.1 y/y, economy-wide, JOLTS 2026-06); if AI is freezing knowledge-work hiring instead, exposed postings should be depressed and they are (-23.1% against their own Feb-2020 level). The second survives the test, the first does not. That is the direction I tested it in, and it points at freeze rather than fire.

*Attribution incentives, both ways.* An employer has reason to say "AI" — it reads as forward-leaning to investors — and reason not to, since AI-attributed layoffs draw political and regulatory attention that "macro headwinds" does not. Neither direction is disinterested, so a report in either direction is a hypothesis. I tested the AI-attribution direction against JTSLDR and the exposed postings index, as above. I tested the macro-attribution direction against the control leg of the jobs panel and the control leg of the postings panel, both of which are healthy, which is what makes a purely macro reading hard to sustain. Both tests ran on series, not on quotes.

**10. Hypotheses considered and rejected**

*CONFOUNDED on interest rates.* Named cause: the tightening cycle, real 10-year at 2.4%, which the postings panel's own artifact says accounts for much of the 2022 opening of the spread. Rejected as a verdict because the contemporaneous test fails it: construction, the most rate-sensitive industry there is, sits in the control leg and is growing at 1.16% y/y, and control postings are above their pre-pandemic level. Rates plausibly explain a slice of the exposed leg (real estate, insurance) and the historical *level* of the postings spread; they do not explain a control leg this healthy. Downgraded to a caveat on attribution rather than a confounder verdict.

*CONFOUNDED on federal contracting / temp help inside professional and business services.* Genuinely plausible and genuinely untestable here — there is no series in this payload that separates temp help or federal contractors from the rest of the exposed leg. "Mixed evidence" and "I can imagine a cause" are not grounds for CONFOUNDED; a named cause needs a supporting series and I do not have one. Logged as a standing weakness of the industry proxy.

*DISPLACEMENT at LOW.* The closest call in this analysis, and the case is set out in full in the inversions above: exposed employment outright negative for a year, exposed postings 23% below their own baseline, U-6 gap at 1.81σ, prime-age 3-month change at 1.95σ, labour share at a record low falling in its fastest decile, the attribution z re-widening as adoption rose, and a frozen-market signature that hides the entrant cohort this dashboard cannot see. What kept me on the other side: the panel that the payload designates as deciding removal-versus-reallocation reads 0.0 on its 12-month change at 0.8σ, below its own attention line, with the level above 2019; the long-term unemployed share, which is the most direct measure of people failing to land, moved 0.6 points against a baseline whose standard deviation is 5.2; and the layoff rate, from an independent survey, is at 1.1 and falling. Removal requires people to stop landing, and on the two most direct measures of landing they have not stopped. I hold that this is reallocation — but I hold it at LOW, and the overturn below is set on the field that would show it to be wrong.

**11. Overturn condition — construction and stress-test**

I read augmentation/reallocation, so my condition must fire toward displacement: the labour market ceasing to absorb.

Primary: `reabsorption.headline.change_over_12_months` at or below **-0.6 percentage points**.

*Can anything but my verdict being wrong carry it there?* Recent range of this field, from the joint table's employment_change_12m column: over the last thirteen listed months it runs from -0.5 (2025-07, 2026-06) to +0.3 (2026-03, 2026-05), with a rough standard deviation around 0.25. **-0.5 has been reached twice in that span with nothing else deteriorating and reversed within a month or two each time, so -0.5 discriminates nothing** and I have deliberately not set it there. -0.6 is beyond anything the observation window has produced since the pandemic ended. It is not reachable by an ordinary rebound (wrong sign), and the field is a 12-month change so a single seasonal month cannot carry it. The Census control re-basing that puts level breaks in both legs each January is the confounder to respect — but it lands in January, outside this 90-day window, and the ratio itself re-bases numerator and denominator together with January steps of 0.2 and 0.1 points, inside its ordinary monthly variation. So a data artefact of that kind cannot reach -0.6 either.

*Can it fire?* Yes. The field moved from +0.3 to -0.5 in a single print between 2026-05 and 2026-06 — an 0.8 swing in one month — so a further 0.6 over three prints is well inside demonstrated behaviour. The 3-month change is already -0.3 and falling at 1.95σ, which is precisely the configuration that would carry the 12-month figure down if it persists. This is a monthly household-survey series with an as_of of 2026-07, so three further observations (August, September, October data) publish before 2026-11-06. This is not a quarterly series that could sleep through its own test window.

Secondary: `exposed_vs_control_jobs.control_value` at or above **0.8 percent year-over-year**. Currently 1.16. This is what buys the discrimination: it requires the control industries — construction, leisure/hospitality, education/health — to still be adding jobs at a healthy clip while the aggregate prime-age employment share falls hard. A general recession would drag control below 0.8 and the compound condition would not fire, which is correct, because a general recession is not what this dashboard is for. Both conditions must hold. Control has run comfortably above 0.8 through the recent record, so this is a live constraint rather than a formality, and it is monthly CES, publishing three more times inside the window.

If that pair fires — prime-age employment share falling at -0.6 or worse while control industries still grow at 0.8%+ — then the outflow from AI-exposed work is no longer landing, and the reallocation reading I have published here is wrong.

**12. Things in this payload that look off, for the record**

- The `what_changed_since_last_analysis` block lists only macro_regime as moving, yet exposed_vs_control_jobs carries a prior_reading of -2.57 at 2026-06 against -2.35 at 2026-07. That is consistent (the July print predates the previous run, which was yesterday), but a reader comparing the two blocks could easily conclude the jobs panel is unchanged month-over-month when it moved 0.22 points between June and July.
- The reabsorption secondaries score 12-month changes against a 2010-2019 baseline whose mean is signed (U-6 gap -0.35/yr, prime-age +0.42/yr) because that decade was a continuous recovery. The panel identified exactly this problem for levels and fixed it for the headline with a 2019 reference; the same distortion is still live in the secondaries' change deviations and inflates both the U-6 figure and the headline's own 12-month deviation. Worth fixing.
- The hires-minus-quits readout publishes the current levels of both legs but no year-ago levels, so its own instruction to "name the moving side" cannot actually be carried out from the payload. That is a gap in the data, not in the intent.
