REASONING_LOG:

**0. What this run is, and how quiet it is**

Run date 2026-08-08; the previous run was 2026-08-07, one day earlier, on the same data month (2026-07). The change list names exactly one moving panel: the 10y-2y spread, 0.4 → 0.5. Everything else is byte-identical to yesterday. So before anything else: the panels have not moved. Whatever I say here is a re-reading of a static picture, not a response to news in the series, and that alone caps confidence. I am told not to see the previous verdict and I have not; I am reasoning from the panels.

I state up front, as required: **my support rests mainly on the absence of deterioration, not on positive evidence of augmentation.** I am reading "workers are moving rather than being removed," not "AI is making exposed workers more valuable." The one panel that would carry the positive claim — exposed pay running 1.0 point ahead of control — is disqualified from carrying it by its own composition artifact (below), and the economy-wide productivity check returned no break. So this is a directional call on the reallocation-vs-removal axis, filed on the augmentation side because the removal signature is absent, and it is LOW for exactly that reason.

**1. exposed_vs_control_jobs (as_of 2026-07, 1 month old) — ATTRIBUTION**

Naming the moving side rather than the gap: exposed industries (information, professional/business, financial) are at **-1.19% year-over-year — an outright contraction**. Control industries (construction, leisure/hospitality, education/health) are at **+1.16%**. The differential is -2.35, prior month -2.57.

Deviation: 1.82σ against the fixed 2010-01..2019-12 window, 0.59σ against full history. The divergence note flags the classic pattern — the reading looks tamer against a window that has swallowed 2023-2026 — so I reason from the pre-2020 figure, 1.82σ. That is past the attention line of 1 and short of the alarm line of 2. The registered trigger is -2.48; last month's -2.57 was past it and this month's -2.35 is not. The panel effectively de-escalated by one notch this month.

Contemporaneous macro test, which is the one that counts: if this were a general downturn, the control leg would be weak too. It is not — control is adding jobs at 1.16% a year, and control postings (below) sit 5.3% *above* their own pre-pandemic level. Note especially that **construction, the most interest-rate-sensitive industry in the economy, sits in the control leg**, and the control leg is healthy while the real 10-year yield is 2.4%. That is the strongest single argument against reading the exposed-side weakness as a pure rate story — though it does not fully clear rates, because the exposed leg carries real estate and insurance, which are rate-sensitive in a different way (asset values and transaction volumes, not construction employment). I cannot separate that from this payload.

Two other non-AI candidates live inside the exposed leg and I want them on the record even though nothing here lets me test either: (a) the 2023 writers'/actors' strikes sit inside the months this differential was widest — the joint table's attribution_z peaks at 5.66 in 2023-11, exactly there, so the historical extreme of this series is partly a labour dispute in motion pictures, with no AI in it; (b) professional and business services contains temporary help and federal contracting, both of which turn early and hard for reasons unrelated to AI. Neither is a series I can point to in this payload, so neither reaches the bar for CONFOUNDED. They are reasons to hold the attribution loosely.

Revision hazard, from the panel's own methodology note: the two most recent CES months are preliminary, the birth-death model misses turning points in both directions, and annual benchmarking has recently run to hundreds of thousands of jobs. So the -1.19/+1.16 pair, and particularly the one-month narrowing from -2.57 to -2.35, is the least reliable part of the series. I am not treating this month's narrowing as a finding; I am treating the four-month flat stretch around -2.3 to -2.6 as the finding.

**The binding weighting rule on this panel is that a widening gap is not displacement.** The mechanics are worked out in the artifact and they are right: 100 jobs destroyed in information and 100 workers hired in health care produces the maximally negative reading here with nobody left behind. So this panel establishes that something is specific to AI-exposed work, and I accept that it does. It cannot establish that work was destroyed.

**Inversion of this panel (it is an attribution panel that cuts against my verdict, so the inversion runs the other way — what is the strongest reading under which it supports ME?):** the gap is *parked, not widening*, and it has fallen back inside its trigger. Over the last four readings it is roughly flat. Against the 2023 peak of 5.66σ it is now 1.82σ — a third as extreme. A divergence that peaked in 2023 and has converged since, while AI capability and adoption both rose steadily, is a poor fit for an AI-driven story and a good fit for the post-ZIRP white-collar retrenchment plus a strike, both of which are dated events unwinding.

**Against my own reading, honestly:** that convergence story breaks if you look at the window over which I actually have an adoption series. Attribution_z bottomed at 0.96 in 2025-11 and has re-widened to 1.84, 1.91, 1.90, 1.94, 2.14, 2.11, 1.82 across 2026-01 through 2026-07, while firm AI adoption rose 17.3 → 21.5%. So over the only nine months where I can put the two series side by side, **the exposed-vs-control gap re-widened as adoption rose.** That is a correlation between two aggregates with no firm-level linkage — the Census survey asks whether a tool is present, not whether any use case made a role redundant, and nothing connects one firm's "yes" to that same firm's headcount — so it licenses no mechanism. But it is the single strongest thing in this payload pointing at displacement, it is why my confidence is LOW rather than MEDIUM, and it is why my overturn condition is set on absorption rather than on something safe.

**2. reabsorption (as_of 2026-07 for household components, 2026-06 for JOLTS) — the panel that decides**

Population: economy-wide throughout. None of this is an exposed-industry figure and I am not treating it as one.

*Headline (binding).* Prime-age employment share 80.4%, **12-month change 0.0**, deviation 0.8σ against the fixed pre-2020 window — below the attention line. Level 0.45 points above its 2019 reference. The two baselines agree here (divergence 0.08), so this reading does not depend on window choice. On the measure the panel designates as placing the axis, absorption is holding.

The decomposition is unusable for magnitudes and says so: both the employed and population legs step through the January Census control re-basing (roughly +1.7m and -1.0m on the employed leg at Jan-2025 and Jan-2026 respectively, against a normal month of 100-200k), so any 12-month change spans a break on both sides. The ratio re-bases numerator and denominator together and is the reliable object. I take only the direction check from it and quote none of the level changes. I also note the payload's own warning: the -779k employed figure here is CPS, ages 25-54, twelve months, and the -23k payroll figure in the news package is CES, all ages, one month. Three things differ at once. They are not netted and neither refutes the other.

*Fast horizon (context only, and the main threat to my verdict).* The 3-month change is **-0.3, at 1.95σ against the clean pre-2020 window** — just short of the alarm line, and it disagrees with the headline. The panel is explicit that this is a hypothesis about a turn rather than a finding, and that a 3-month move on a noisy monthly series must not move a verdict by itself. I am citing the 12-month horizon for the verdict and flagging the 3-month as the reason I am at LOW and the reason my overturn sits on this exact field. If the fast horizon is the truth arriving early, I am wrong within a quarter, which is precisely the outcome the overturn machinery exists to record.

*Layoffs and hiring, read as a pair as the panel demands.* Layoffs and discharges 1.1, 12-month change -0.1, deviation -0.34σ (away from displacement) and the 3-month at -0.94σ. Hires 3.4, quits 2.0, net 1.4, 12-month change +0.1, deviation -0.90σ (away from displacement). Read together per the panel's rule: layoffs at or below norm alongside unspectacular hiring is a **FROZEN market, not a cyclical contraction**. Firms are not shedding incumbents; they are not replacing exits. That distinction matters enormously here, because it tells me the -1.19% in exposed industries is very likely attrition and hiring freeze rather than discharge — and *that is compatible with both my verdict and the opposite one*, which I take up in the inversion.

Naming the moving side on hires-minus-quits, as required: the net rose 0.1 over twelve months, but the payload gives me only current levels (3.4 and 2.0) and the net's change, not each side's year-ago level. **I cannot tell whether the net improved because hiring picked up or because quitting fell further.** A rising hires-minus-quits driven by collapsing quits is workers afraid to move, not a market absorbing people, and it would read as improvement on this readout. That is an unresolved question inside a panel I am leaning on, and it weakens the readout materially. I am not going to pretend otherwise.

*Long-term unemployed share.* 25.5%, +0.6 points over twelve months, 0.31σ — essentially nothing against a baseline whose standard deviation is 5.2 points. Exits are still being caught reasonably quickly. This is the readout that would light up first if people who left exposed work were failing to land, and it has not.

*Underemployment gap (U-6 minus U-3).* 3.8, +0.2 over twelve months, **1.81σ against the fixed window**, though the 3-month change is -0.1 (improving) and sits at 0.0σ. This is the displacement-side readout on this panel and I take it seriously as the "landing badly" channel. One caveat I want on the record, from the panel's own construction: the baseline for 12-month *changes* here is drawn from 2010-2019, a decade of continuously narrowing underemployment (mean change -0.35 per year). Against a decade that improved every year, a +0.2 year scores as 1.8σ of deterioration when in level terms it is a move from 3.6 to 3.8. The panel explicitly acknowledged this problem for *levels* and fixed it for the headline by using a 2019 reference point instead; it did not apply the same fix to the change baselines on the secondaries. So I read the 1.81σ as real but inflated by the baseline decade's direction, and I note the fast horizon is going the other way.

*Vintage inside the panel.* Household series to 2026-07, JOLTS to 2026-06. One month, stated, immaterial — but it means a very recent turn would appear in the headline before it appeared in layoffs and hiring, and the headline's fast horizon is the thing that is wobbling. Worth holding.

*Joint position.* 34 of 42 observation months sit outside the 2σ baseline joint range, against 11 of 120 baseline months. That is a genuine finding about the period as a whole: this combination of readings is unusual against the 2010s. But it is dominated by 2023-2024, when attribution_z ran 3-5 with the strikes inside it, and the most recent month (2026-07: z 1.82, employment change 0.0) is back *inside* the baseline range. Months 2026-04, -05 and -06 were outside. It flickers. Also noted, per the panel's instruction: 2025-10 is absent from the table entirely, so any slope drawn across that point is drawn across more than a month.

**Inversion of the reabsorption panel — the best version of the case that these same numbers support DISPLACEMENT:**

- A flat aggregate employment ratio is exactly what *successful reabsorption into worse work* looks like, and the U-6 gap widening 1.81σ is what that would leave behind. Perfect displacement with everyone re-employed part-time or below their skill produces a flat headline and a widening U-6. My headline reading cannot distinguish that from health, and the one readout designed to catch it is the one at 1.8σ.
- The ratio is restricted to ages 25-54 *on purpose*, which is the right call for retirements but blinds it to a displacement episode that falls on entrants. And the frozen-market signature I just described — low layoffs, unreplaced exits — is precisely the shape that pushes the whole burden onto people trying to get in. Nobody aged 22-24 is in this panel. If AI is eating entry-level knowledge work, this dashboard would show me a flat prime-age ratio, a low layoff rate, and a depressed exposed-postings index, which is exactly what it is showing me. **I regard this as the strongest argument against my verdict and I do not have a panel that answers it.** It is a reason for LOW, and if the payload ever gains a 20-24 employment series it may reverse this reading outright.
- Low and falling layoffs is not evidence against displacement at all. AI-driven job removal via attrition and hiring freeze never touches JTSLDR. So my second-best corroborating readout only rules out the cyclical-shedding variety of displacement, not the variety this dashboard exists to detect.
- The 3-month headline change at 1.95σ can be read as the turn already beginning, with the 12-month window not yet able to show it.

I have weighed all four. What holds me on the augmentation side is that the removal signature requires people to *stop landing*, and the two readouts that measure landing directly — long-term unemployed share (0.31σ) and the layoff rate (-0.34σ) — are both quiet, and the second of those comes from JOLTS, a genuinely different instrument from the household survey that produces the other three. If people were being removed at the scale implied by -1.19% across three large sectors for a year, I would expect the long-term unemployed share to have moved more than 0.6 points.

**3. job_postings_spread (as_of 2026-07) — ATTRIBUTION, earliest-moving**

Naming both sides against their own baselines, as required, before any spread: **exposed knowledge-work postings sit at 76.9, i.e. 23.1% below their own February 2020 level. Control hands-on postings sit at 105.3, 5.3% above theirs.** That is a standing, severe depression in advertised knowledge-work demand alongside healthy hands-on demand. It is strong attribution — a general contraction pulls both legs down and this has not — and it is the second instrument, on a different cut (occupation, not industry) and from a different source (Indeed, not BLS), agreeing that the weakness is specific to knowledge work. I weight the occupational cut *above* the industry cut on exposure, since a janitor in the information sector is not exposed and a data analyst in manufacturing is.

The panel's binding weighting rule is to read the change, not the level, because the spread opened in 2022 — before current tools diffused into hiring, and coincident with the tightening cycle rather than with any model release. So: **spread_change_over_6_months = +2.6**, i.e. narrowing. Against its own (contaminated, 2023-onward) history the current -28.4 is -1.17σ, on the away-from-displacement side of a mean of -33.5. The exposed side has not been getting worse over six months.

The panel also states plainly what it is not: hands-on strength is a fact about hands-on work and says nothing about whether exposed workers are being made more valuable; augmentation on this panel would be knowledge-work postings recovering *toward their own baseline*. At 76.9 they have not recovered. So this panel gives me "not deteriorating," not "improving," and certainly not augmentation.

**Inversion:** the spread can narrow because exposed postings recovered *or because control postings fell*, and the payload gives me each side's level but not each side's six-month change — **so I cannot name the moving side on the thing I am actually citing.** If the narrowing came from control weakening, that is a deteriorating economy misread as an exposed-side recovery, and it would support the opposite verdict. Second inversion: 2.6 points off a -33.5 average is small relative to the series' 4.37 standard deviation, so it may be noise. Third: postings lead employment, and a leading indicator that has been sitting 23% below baseline for years is a standing prediction of continued weakness in exposed hiring regardless of which way the last six months wobbled. I accept all three. This panel is the third leg of my reading and the weakest of the three.

**4. exposed_vs_control_wages (as_of 2026-07) — cited, NOT leaned on**

Exposed pay +4.22% y/y, control +3.21%, differential +1.00 (prior 0.93), deviation -0.60σ (away from displacement), 24 consecutive readings inside its 2010s range. Exposed workers' average pay is pulling ahead, which on its face is the augmentation signature.

**I am not leaning on it, and here is why in my own words.** The panel's own field says exposed employment is falling at -1.19%. This is an average over a group whose membership is changing while the group shrinks. If entry-level hiring in exposed industries has stopped — which is exactly what the frozen-market reading of the JOLTS pair and the -23% exposed postings index both imply — then the juniors have left the denominator and the average rises with nobody receiving a raise. A genuine pay story and the composition story predict the identical observation, and nothing in this payload separates them. The control leg has the mirror problem in the opposite direction: it contains leisure and hospitality, low-wage and growing, which drags the control average down mechanically. So both legs of this differential are moving for reasons that have nothing to do with what any individual is paid.

The designated cross-check, individual_wage_growth, is economy-wide and cannot be cut to exposed industries, so it cannot resolve this. It can only tell me the aggregate reading is not being contradicted, and it isn't: stayers 3.6%, switchers 4.4%, premium 0.8, inside its pre-2020 range (mean 0.58, sd 0.41), deviation -0.54σ, recovering over the last four readings. Composition cannot move that series because it follows the same people twelve months apart. So: economy-wide, people who change jobs are still getting paid more for it, at a normal premium. That is the cleanest available evidence that movers are landing *well* — and "landing well" is the part the reabsorption panel cannot see.

**Inversion of individual_wage_growth:** the switcher premium is itself a selection statistic, as the panel says — if the weaker candidates lose the ability to move at all, the median switcher's gain rises while the marginal worker's outcome collapses. It is a *median*, so a collapse concentrated in a minority of workers is precisely the shape it would miss, and an early displacement episode is exactly that shape. It is economy-wide, so it can never be evidence about AI-exposed work. It is CPS-based through a period of degraded response rates, with October 2025 missing outright at source, and it is 2 months old. I accept all of that: it is a corroborating panel of modest weight, not a pillar.

**5. labor_productivity (as_of 2026-06) — GAINS_TEST, economy-wide**

2.2%, down from 2.9%. Above the pre-2020 mean of 1.27 by 0.83σ, but **below the panel's 2.7-3.4 "internet-boom" band and far below the 3.4-for-two-quarters break rule. One reading below the band.** So: no productivity break. The gains AI is supposed to deliver are not visible in the aggregate at the scale that would make the augmentation story affirmative.

**Inversion, and it is sharp:** if productivity gains *were* AI-driven and concentrated in exposed industries while exposed hours fell -1.19%, then output-per-hour rising is the *displacement* arithmetic — the same output from fewer hours — not the augmentation one. An economy-wide aggregate cannot tell those apart, and it is heavily revised besides. So this panel does not support my verdict; it returns "no break," which is consistent with augmentation being too new to register, with there being no gains, and with gains arriving through headcount reduction. I count it as a check that failed to find positive evidence for my side, and I say so rather than dressing 0.83σ above a 2010s mean up as an AI dividend.

**6. worker_share_of_income (as_of 2026-03, 5 months old) — DESCRIPTIVE, no vote, economy-wide**

51.0% of gross domestic income, which is **below the previous full-history low of 51.19 (2025-12) in a series running back to 1947**. Four consecutive quarterly declines. 4-quarter change -1.0, in the fastest 10% of declines on record. One-year drift -0.96/yr against a 40-year pace of -0.13/yr — roughly seven times the secular rate.

This panel votes on nothing and I am not putting it in the load-bearing list, but I am not going to leave a genuine finding out either: a record low, falling in its fastest decile, is worth saying out loud. The weakness I am accepting in order to say it: it is economy-wide, so it cannot attribute anything to AI-exposed work; the share has fallen for forty years for causes predating AI; the panel's own note points out that ordinary recessions produced faster falls (-2.18 in 2009, -1.59 in 2010), so "falling fast" is normally a business-cycle statement. What makes this one non-trivial is that **we are not in a recession** — unemployment 4.1%, payrolls roughly flat, yield curve positive at +0.5 — and a fastest-decile fall in labour share outside a recession is not the usual pattern. It is 5 months old, a gap of four months against the 2026-07 panels, which is the one comparison in this analysis that exceeds a quarter, and I flag it: **the main evidence arguing against my verdict on this axis is older than the evidence supporting it**, so it cannot yet reflect any recent turn in either direction. If Q2 lands at 50.x with the labour market still calm, that hardens the displacement case considerably.

**7. ai_adoption (as_of 2026-07) — deployment context**

21.5% of firms, up from 20.6, and up steadily from 17.3% in 2025-11. Size gradient: 20.8% at 1-4 employees against 36.8% at 250+, ratio 1.77, so worker exposure is meaningfully higher than the firm-count headline (no employment weights are published and I am not going to invent a worker-weighted percentage).

What I take from it: deployment is real and rising, which removes the objection that an AI explanation is unavailable. What I do not take from it: any evidence that anyone lost work. The survey asks whether a tool is present in any business function, not whether a use case made a role redundant, and there is no firm-level linkage — nothing connects a given firm's "yes" to that firm's hiring freeze. It is self-reported by firms with a reason to look forward-leaning, over a respondent panel that rotates between collections, so month-to-month moves can be a change in who answered. A rise here removes an objection; it supplies no reason.

The one thing I did do with it is the timing check in section 1: adoption rose 17.3 → 21.5% over the same nine months in which the attribution z re-widened from 0.96 to 1.82. Two aggregates moving together, no mechanism, but I logged it because it cuts against me.

**8. Panels that contribute nothing, read anyway**

*ai_capability_metr* (2026-04): frontier 80% horizon 186 minutes. The task suite is clean, self-contained, auto-scorable software and cyber problems with contractor baselines and no prior context; horizons past ~960 minutes are beyond what it can score. The dashboard's own 2400-minute "working week" bar sits 2.5x past the instrument ceiling, and the naive 2027-10 crossing is one of four fits that disagree materially. None of this is an event in anyone's employment. Noted, counted in nothing.

*ai_capability_gdpval_ratings* (2026-08): Claude Opus 5 at 1846 Elo, 104 points clear of the next model. Model-versus-model with no human in the pool, so levels mean nothing and only differences carry information. Which lab leads is not a step in any chain that ends in a job.

*ai_capability_vs_human_experts* (2025-12, 8 months stale): 70.9% wins-plus-ties, and the parity caveat matters — true parity is wins-only, where the figure is 49.7%, and the number is OpenAI reporting on OpenAI's own benchmark. Nothing published since 2025-12; the gap is an instrument gap, not a capability statement. This is the most persuasive-looking capability panel because there is a human on the other side, which is the reason to handle it carefully rather than a reason to weight it. Clearing an expert on a benchmark task is not an employer deciding to stop paying that expert.

*ai_use_automation_vs_augmentation* (2025-09, 11 months stale): 43.1/56.9, essentially unmoved across three releases. It is one vendor's conversations over a user base that changes between releases, and it is the stalest panel here while measuring the fastest-moving thing on the dashboard — it predates every labor month I am reading by most of a year. The only thing worth saying is that the split was stable over the releases that exist. It plays no part in the verdict.

*macro_regime* (2026-08): real 10-year 2.4%, 10y-2y +0.5 (up from 0.4, the only change since the last run), expected inflation 2.3%, **curve not inverted**. This can name a competing cause; it cannot clear one, because it prices expectations rather than history. What I use it for: the bond market is not pricing an ordinary recession, so the cyclical hypothesis does not get free corroboration here — but I explicitly do not use the non-inverted curve to exculpate the exposed-side weakness already sitting in the CES and Indeed data. The contemporaneous test is the one I ran, in section 1, on the control legs, and it came back saying the weakness is not general.

**9. News package**

*BLS Employment Situation, through 2026-07:* nonfarm payrolls 158,858k, **-23k on the month**; unemployment 4.1%. This is economy-wide, all ages, establishment survey, one month. It is soft, and it fits the frozen-market reading (low layoffs, unreplaced exits) better than either a boom or a shedding contraction. It does not distinguish exposed from control, so it cannot move an attribution reading, and one preliminary month of CES is the least reliable object on offer. It does *not* refute the flat prime-age employment ratio and I have not netted the two: different survey, different age range, different horizon. Revisions to prior months are legitimate veto material and I would watch them, but none are reported here.

*AP wire, Iran war / energy / mortgages / job openings:* a war can move energy prices, inflation expectations and hiring. Two reasons it does not move this verdict. First, timing — it is too recent to be inside the June and July industry data at any scale, and it cannot explain a knowledge-work postings deficit that has been sitting at 20-30% since 2022. Second, shape — an energy and confidence shock hits consumer-facing, transport and energy-intensive work, most of which is in my control leg, and the control leg is the healthy one. If a war shock were driving this, the divergence would run the other way. The mortgage/rates thread is more interesting, because it is a live confounder for the real-estate and insurance component of the exposed leg, and real yields at 2.4% are not accommodative. What limits it is that the most rate-sensitive industry in the economy, construction, sits in the *control* leg and is growing. So rates can explain part of the exposed leg and cannot explain the control leg's health. Noted, not sufficient for CONFOUNDED, because I cannot point to a series in this payload that isolates it.

*NY Fed Liberty Street, "AI's Impact on Labor and Hiring":* a hypothesis generator, and I have only the title. Whatever it concludes is published analysis about some period, not a measurement of this quarter, and I will not substitute a remembered or inferred finding for the series in front of me. What I did instead was ask what such a piece would predict and test it here: if employers are cutting because of AI, the discharge rate should be rising and it is falling (1.1, -0.1 y/y, economy-wide, JOLTS 2026-06); if AI is freezing knowledge-work hiring instead, exposed postings should be depressed and they are (-23.1% against their own Feb-2020 level). The second survives the test, the first does not. That is the direction I tested it in, and it points at freeze rather than fire.

*Attribution incentives, both ways.* An employer has reason to say "AI" — it reads as forward-leaning to investors — and reason not to, since AI-attributed layoffs draw political and regulatory attention that "macro headwinds" does not. Neither direction is disinterested, so a report in either direction is a hypothesis. I tested the AI-attribution direction against JTSLDR and the exposed postings index, as above. I tested the macro-attribution direction against the control leg of the jobs panel and the control leg of the postings panel, both of which are healthy, which is what makes a purely macro reading hard to sustain. Both tests ran on series, not on quotes.

**10. Hypotheses considered and rejected**

*CONFOUNDED on interest rates.* Named cause: the tightening cycle, real 10-year at 2.4%, which the postings panel's own artifact says accounts for much of the 2022 opening of the spread. Rejected as a verdict because the contemporaneous test fails it: construction, the most rate-sensitive industry there is, sits in the control leg and is growing at 1.16% y/y, and control postings are above their pre-pandemic level. Rates plausibly explain a slice of the exposed leg (real estate, insurance) and the historical *level* of the postings spread; they do not explain a control leg this healthy. Downgraded to a caveat on attribution rather than a confounder verdict.

*CONFOUNDED on federal contracting / temp help inside professional and business services.* Genuinely plausible and genuinely untestable here — there is no series in this payload that separates temp help or federal contractors from the rest of the exposed leg. "Mixed evidence" and "I can imagine a cause" are not grounds for CONFOUNDED; a named cause needs a supporting series and I do not have one. Logged as a standing weakness of the industry proxy.

*DISPLACEMENT at LOW.* The closest call in this analysis, and the case is set out in full in the inversions above: exposed employment outright negative for a year, exposed postings 23% below their own baseline, U-6 gap at 1.81σ, prime-age 3-month change at 1.95σ, labour share at a record low falling in its fastest decile, the attribution z re-widening as adoption rose, and a frozen-market signature that hides the entrant cohort this dashboard cannot see. What kept me on the other side: the panel that the payload designates as deciding removal-versus-reallocation reads 0.0 on its 12-month change at 0.8σ, below its own attention line, with the level above 2019; the long-term unemployed share, which is the most direct measure of people failing to land, moved 0.6 points against a baseline whose standard deviation is 5.2; and the layoff rate, from an independent survey, is at 1.1 and falling. Removal requires people to stop landing, and on the two most direct measures of landing they have not stopped. I hold that this is reallocation — but I hold it at LOW, and the overturn below is set on the field that would show it to be wrong.

**11. Overturn condition — construction and stress-test**

I read augmentation/reallocation, so my condition must fire toward displacement: the labour market ceasing to absorb.

Primary: `reabsorption.headline.change_over_12_months` at or below **-0.6 percentage points**.

*Can anything but my verdict being wrong carry it there?* Recent range of this field, from the joint table's employment_change_12m column: over the last thirteen listed months it runs from -0.5 (2025-07, 2026-06) to +0.3 (2026-03, 2026-05), with a rough standard deviation around 0.25. **-0.5 has been reached twice in that span with nothing else deteriorating and reversed within a month or two each time, so -0.5 discriminates nothing** and I have deliberately not set it there. -0.6 is beyond anything the observation window has produced since the pandemic ended. It is not reachable by an ordinary rebound (wrong sign), and the field is a 12-month change so a single seasonal month cannot carry it. The Census control re-basing that puts level breaks in both legs each January is the confounder to respect — but it lands in January, outside this 90-day window, and the ratio itself re-bases numerator and denominator together with January steps of 0.2 and 0.1 points, inside its ordinary monthly variation. So a data artefact of that kind cannot reach -0.6 either.

*Can it fire?* Yes. The field moved from +0.3 to -0.5 in a single print between 2026-05 and 2026-06 — an 0.8 swing in one month — so a further 0.6 over three prints is well inside demonstrated behaviour. The 3-month change is already -0.3 and falling at 1.95σ, which is precisely the configuration that would carry the 12-month figure down if it persists. This is a monthly household-survey series with an as_of of 2026-07, so three further observations (August, September, October data) publish before 2026-11-06. This is not a quarterly series that could sleep through its own test window.

Secondary: `exposed_vs_control_jobs.control_value` at or above **0.8 percent year-over-year**. Currently 1.16. This is what buys the discrimination: it requires the control industries — construction, leisure/hospitality, education/health — to still be adding jobs at a healthy clip while the aggregate prime-age employment share falls hard. A general recession would drag control below 0.8 and the compound condition would not fire, which is correct, because a general recession is not what this dashboard is for. Both conditions must hold. Control has run comfortably above 0.8 through the recent record, so this is a live constraint rather than a formality, and it is monthly CES, publishing three more times inside the window.

If that pair fires — prime-age employment share falling at -0.6 or worse while control industries still grow at 0.8%+ — then the outflow from AI-exposed work is no longer landing, and the reallocation reading I have published here is wrong.

**12. Things in this payload that look off, for the record**

- The `what_changed_since_last_analysis` block lists only macro_regime as moving, yet exposed_vs_control_jobs carries a prior_reading of -2.57 at 2026-06 against -2.35 at 2026-07. That is consistent (the July print predates the previous run, which was yesterday), but a reader comparing the two blocks could easily conclude the jobs panel is unchanged month-over-month when it moved 0.22 points between June and July.
- The reabsorption secondaries score 12-month changes against a 2010-2019 baseline whose mean is signed (U-6 gap -0.35/yr, prime-age +0.42/yr) because that decade was a continuous recovery. The panel identified exactly this problem for levels and fixed it for the headline with a 2019 reference; the same distortion is still live in the secondaries' change deviations and inflates both the U-6 figure and the headline's own 12-month deviation. Worth fixing.
- The hires-minus-quits readout publishes the current levels of both legs but no year-ago levels, so its own instruction to "name the moving side" cannot actually be carried out from the payload. That is a gap in the data, not in the intent.

pass2.notificationLine: Only the yield curve moved; no-displacement reading holds on absent damage, not gains.
pass2.publishedNote:
AI-exposed work is shrinking, but the people leaving it still appear to be landing in other jobs — reallocation rather than removal — and that reading rests on the absence of damage, not on any evidence that AI is making exposed workers more productive or better paid.

Nothing moved this month. Twelve of thirteen panels carry identical numbers to the last read. The single change is the gap between ten-year and two-year Treasury yields, from 0.4 to 0.5 points, which says the bond market is not pricing a recession and says nothing about AI.

What holds the reallocation reading up: people who lose work are still finding it. The share of 25-to-54-year-olds with a job is 80.4%, unchanged over twelve months and about half a point above its 2019 level. Of everyone unemployed, 25.5% have been out more than six months, up just 0.6 points on the year against a measure that normally swings by several points. Layoffs are running at 1.1% of employment a month and falling. Employers are not throwing people out; they are declining to replace those who leave. All three of those figures cover the whole economy, not AI-exposed workers specifically, which is a real limit on what they can prove.

What argues hard the other way, and it is a lot. Employment in AI-exposed industries — information, professional services, finance — is falling at 1.19% a year, an outright contraction, while construction, hospitality, education and health are adding jobs at 1.16%. Postings for knowledge work sit about 23% below their February 2020 level; postings for hands-on work are about 5% above theirs. Labour's share of all income in the economy is 51.0%, the lowest in a series running back to 1947, down four quarters straight and falling at a pace normally seen only in recessions — and unemployment is 4.1%, so this is not a recession. That reading is from March, five months old, so the strongest evidence against this verdict is older than the evidence for it.

Two more. pass2.fullAnalysis:
The reading this month is that AI-exposed work is shrinking but the people leaving it are still landing in jobs — reallocation rather than removal. That reading rests almost entirely on the absence of damage, not on evidence that AI is making exposed workers more productive or better paid. It is held with low confidence, and the case against it is substantial enough that it takes up as much room below as the case for.

WHAT ACTUALLY CHANGED

Almost nothing. Since the last read, twelve of the thirteen panels carry byte-identical numbers. The single move is in bond yields: the gap between ten-year and two-year Treasuries went from 0.4 to 0.5 points. That gap being positive rather than negative means the bond market is not pricing an ordinary recession. It says nothing whatever about AI, and it does not touch any employment series. Everything else here is yesterday's picture, re-read.

THE CASE FOR REALLOCATION

Three things say people are still landing.

The share of 25-to-54-year-olds with a job is 80.4%, which is exactly where it was twelve months ago and about half a point above where it stood in 2019. If a large group of workers were being pushed out of employment altogether, this is where it would show, and it has not moved.

Of everyone unemployed, 25.5% have been out of work more than six months. That is up 0.6 points over the year, against a measure that routinely swings by several points. When people who lose jobs cannot find new ones, this figure climbs hard. It has barely twitched.

Layoffs and discharges are running at 1.1% of employment a month, slightly lower than a year ago. Hiring is at 3.4% and quits at 2.0%. Read together, that is a frozen market rather than a shrinking one: employers are not throwing people out, they are declining to replace the ones who leave. This comes from a survey of employers, a genuinely separate instrument from the household survey that produces the other two figures, and it agrees with them.

All three of these numbers cover the whole economy, every industry and both sexes and all sectors — not AI-exposed workers specifically. That is an important limit. They can tell you that the economy as a whole is absorbing people. They cannot tell you that the specific people leaving information, professional services and finance are the ones being absorbed.

One economy-wide figure does speak to how movers fare: people who changed employers over the past year got pay rises of 4.4%, against 3.6% for people who stayed put. That premium is normal by pre-2020 standards, and because it follows the same individuals a year apart, it cannot be manufactured by changes in who is in the sample. Job-changing still pays. That is the closest thing here to direct evidence that people who move land well.

THE CASE AGAINST, AT FULL STRENGTH

Employment in AI-exposed industries — information, professional and business services, finance — is falling at 1.19% a year. That is an outright contraction, not slower growth. Meanwhile the control industries — construction, leisure and hospitality, education and health — are adding jobs at 1.16% a year. The weakness is specific, not general.

Advertised demand tells the same story on a different cut and from a different source. Postings for knowledge work sit about 23% below their February 2020 level. Postings for hands-on work sit about 5% above theirs. A knowledge-work hiring market a fifth smaller than before the pandemic, for years running, is a standing forecast of continued weakness in exposed hiring.

Labour's share of all income generated in the economy is 51.0%, which is the lowest reading in a series that begins in 1947 — below the previous record set only last December. It has fallen four quarters running, and the fall over the past year is among the fastest tenth on record. Falls this fast normally happen in recessions, and we are not in one: unemployment is 4.1% and payrolls are roughly flat. A record low in labour's share, falling at recession speed outside a recession, is a genuine finding and I am not going to bury it. Two caveats belong with it, and neither dissolves it. This share has drifted down for forty years for reasons that long predate AI. And this reading is from March 2026, five months old — the newest evidence arguing against the reallocation reading is older than the evidence supporting it, which means it cannot yet reflect any recent turn either way.

The exposed-versus-control jobs gap was at its narrowest in November of last year and has been wider in every month since, across the same nine months in which the share of firms reporting AI use rose from 17.3% to 21.5%. Two aggregates moving together prove nothing — the adoption survey asks whether a tool is present somewhere in the business, not whether any role was made redundant, and nothing links a particular firm's "yes" to that firm's hiring — but it is the single strongest thing in this data pointing the other way, and it is the main reason confidence is low.

The employment share that carries most of the weight here covers ages 25 to 54, on purpose, to keep retirements out. That also makes it blind to people trying to enter the workforce. And a frozen market — few layoffs, unfilled vacancies — is exactly the shape that pushes the whole cost onto entrants. If AI is eating junior knowledge work, this data would show a flat prime-age employment share, low layoffs and depressed knowledge-work postings, which is precisely what it does show. There is no panel here that answers this, and it is the strongest single objection to the reallocation reading.

Finally, the prime-age employment share has been drifting down over the last three months, by 0.3 points, even as the twelve-month change sits at zero. Three months on a noisy monthly series is a hypothesis about a turn, not a turn. But it is the configuration that would drag the twelve-month figure down if it persists, and it is why the condition that would overturn this reading is set on that exact number.

THE PAY PANEL, AND WHY IT IS NOT EVIDENCE

Average pay in AI-exposed industries is growing at 4.22% a year against 3.21% in the control industries. On its face that is the augmentation signature: exposed workers getting more valuable, not less. I am not treating it as evidence, and the reason is on the same panel. Exposed employment is falling at 1.19% a year, and the postings data says entry-level hiring in those industries has largely stopped. When juniors stop being hired, they drop out of the average and the average rises without anybody getting a raise. The control side has the mirror problem: it contains leisure and hospitality, low-paid and growing, which drags its average down mechanically. A real pay story and a pure composition artefact predict the identical number, and nothing available separates them.

ALTERNATIVES CONSIDERED AND REJECTED

Interest rates. Borrowing costs are genuinely restrictive — the ten-year yield is about 2.4% after inflation — and much of the knowledge-work postings collapse dates to 2022, when the tightening cycle began, not to any model release. But construction, the most rate-sensitive industry in the economy, sits in the control group, and construction and its peers are growing at 1.16% a year with hands-on postings above their pre-pandemic level. Rates plausibly explain part of the exposed side, particularly real estate and insurance. They cannot explain a control side this healthy. So rates are a caveat on attribution, not the explanation.

A general downturn. Same test, same answer: a general contraction pulls both sides down, and only one side is down. July payrolls did fall by 23,000, which is soft, but that is one preliminary month covering the whole economy and it does not distinguish exposed from control work.

Federal contracting and temporary help. Professional and business services contains both, and both turn early and hard for reasons with no AI in them. This is plausible and, with the data at hand, untestable — there is no series that separates them out. It is a standing weakness in using industries as a proxy for AI exposure, and it is logged as one rather than promoted to an explanation.

The 2023 writers' and actors' strikes. The exposed-versus-control gap was at its most extreme in late 2023, exactly when a labour dispute in motion pictures was suppressing employment in the information sector. That matters for reading the history: the peak of this series is partly a strike, and the gap today is roughly a third as extreme as that peak.

WHAT THE PRODUCTIVITY DATA SAYS, WHICH IS NOTHING HELPFUL

Output per hour is growing at 2.2%, down from 2.9%. That is better than the 2010s average of about 1.3%, but well short of the 1990s internet-boom pace and short of anything that would count as a break in trend. If AI were delivering large measurable gains, this is where they would surface, and they have not. Worse, this measure could not tell you which story it supported if it did move: rising output per hour with falling hours in exposed industries is the arithmetic of replacement just as much as of augmentation. It is a check that failed to find positive evidence for the reallocation reading, and I am counting it that way rather than dressing it up.

TWO GAPS IN THE DATA WORTH KNOWING ABOUT

The hiring and quits figures are published as current levels with a change in their difference, but without last year's levels for each. That means it is impossible to say whether the small improvement in hiring-minus-quitting came from more hiring or from fewer people daring to quit. Those are opposite stories — a market absorbing people versus workers too frightened to move — and both read as improvement on this measure. That is an unresolved question inside a panel this reading leans on.

And the household employment figures step through an annual population re-basing each January, which puts artificial jumps in the underlying counts of employed people and of the population. The employment share itself is safe because both parts of the ratio are re-based together, which is why this analysis quotes the share and not the underlying counts.

WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT

If the share of 25-to-54-year-olds in work falls by 0.6 points or more over twelve months while the control industries are still adding jobs at 0.8% a year or better, the outflow from AI-exposed work has stopped landing, and the reallocation reading published here is wrong. Both halves matter: a general recession would drag the control industries down too, and a general recession is a different thing from AI displacement. That employment share moved by 0.8 points in a single monthly print earlier this year, so a move of this size in a quarter is well within what the series does.

The run requirement is the newer half and it is what stops the vertical axis deciding this grid on its own: one month past the line used to establish this axis, the gap has been past the line since 2023, and the result was that the only thing ever changing the quadrant was an economy-wide employment change that an ordinary recession moves
definitions.deteriorating: the prime-age (25-54) employment-population ratio is LOWER than it was twelve months ago. A change against raw zero, with no baseline, no reference year and no threshold, because those were all the wrong kind of answer here: a level against 2019 anchored the boundary to a cyclical peak and would have read displacement across most of the 2010s, and z-scoring the change against 2010-2019 scored a mature expansion against a decade of recovery. Zero involves no distribution, so nothing can contaminate it.

path.lineRationale: Both axes cross at zero, and zero is a fact about each measure rather than a chosen threshold: the gap sitting at its own 2010s norm, and employment flat year-over-year. Validated before adoption — this never calls the 2014-2019 boom displacement.

runs.computedDissent: The analyst read AUGMENTATION from the panels without being shown either mechanical reading, and the four-corner grid places this month at DISPLACEMENT (gap wide and holding, aggregate deteriorating). Recorded, not resolved: these are different routes through the same data, and neither one overrules the other. The grid in particular turns on a single economy-wide series sitting near zero, so a month's disagreement with it is ordinary rather than a mark against either reading.

pass1.confidenceBasis: Corroborating: reabsorption (headline prime-age employment share 12-month change 0.0 at 0.8σ, below its attention line; layoffs rate 1.1 and falling; hires 3.4 vs quits 2.0 with the net rising 0.1 over 12 months), exposed_vs_control_wages (exposed pay +4.22% vs control +3.21%, deviation −0.60 i.e. away from displacement), job_postings_spread (spread_change_over_6_months +2.9, narrowing). Refuting or failing to corroborate: exposed_vs_control_jobs (exposed employment outright negative at −1.19% y/y, 1.82σ past its attention line on the clean pre-2020 baseline), labor_productivity (2.2% and decelerating from 2.9%, below the 2.7 band — the augmentation gains test does not corroborate), reabsorption secondary U6−U3 (+0.2, 1.81σ toward displacement) and the headline's own 3-month change (−0.3, 1.95σ) which disagree with the 12-month figure, worker_share_of_income (−0.96 over one year, fastest 10% of declines on record, to a post-1947 low). Doubt unmet: my positive-evidence leg is thin and partly unresolvable — with exposed employment falling, the wage panel's own weighting rule says composition and a genuine pay story predict the same observation, and the composition control is economy-wide so it cannot settle it for exposed industries; the reading therefore rests mainly on absence of deterioration.

falsifier.unit: percentage points (12-month change in the share of 25-54-year-olds with a job)

pass1.falsifierPlain: The prime-age employment-share chart moves first — if its 12-month change falls to −0.6 points or lower by 10 November while control-industry job growth is still at or above 0.8 percent, the exposed outflow is no longer landing anywhere and this reading was wrong.
pass1.reasoningLog:
**Framing up front, because it decides how this should be read.** I am calling AUGMENTATION, and the support for it is mostly the *absence of deterioration* rather than positive evidence that AI-exposed workers are being made more valuable. Prime-age employment is flat, layoffs are low and falling, hiring exceeds quitting and the gap is widening in the healthy direction. That is "displacement has not removed people," not "augmentation is visibly working." There is one strand of genuinely positive evidence — exposed-industry pay running a full point ahead of control — and it is the single weakest panel on the dashboard for exactly the situation we are in. So: thin reading, published thin.

**This was a quiet run.** Of thirteen panels, two headline numbers moved since 2026-08-08: the postings spread by −0.3 (one month, on a series with a 4.39 standard deviation over its short history — noise), and a GDPval Elo by +2.6 (a model-vs-model comparison that is not an event in anybody's employment). Everything else is unchanged. Nothing in "what changed" carries information about workers. When the panels have not moved, the correct output is a directional call at LOW, and that is what this is.

---

**Panel by panel.**

*exposed_vs_control_jobs (ATTRIBUTION, as_of 2026-07, 1 month old).* Naming the moving side rather than the gap: exposed industries are at **−1.19% year-over-year — an outright contraction**, and control industries at **+1.16% — healthy growth**. This is not a gap that opened because control boomed; the exposed leg is shrinking in absolute terms. Differential −2.35, which sits 1.82σ toward displacement against the fixed 2010-2019 window and only 0.59σ against full history. I reason from the pre-2020 figure, as the divergence note directs and as the logic requires: the full-history window contains 2023 onward, which is the period under test, so it has already absorbed the thing being judged into its definition of normal. 1.82σ is past the attention line and short of the alarm line.

Two things temper it. First, the differential moved *away* from the −2.48 trigger this month (−2.57 → −2.35), and the attribution_z path in the joint table shows 1.94 → 2.14 → 2.11 → 1.82 across April to July: elevated, not accelerating. And the longer arc is a decline from 5.66 in November 2023. Second, the composition of these industry codes. "Information" contains publishing, broadcasting, telecom and motion picture — the 2023 peak in this differential sits exactly on top of the writers' and actors' strikes, which is a warning about what this code can do with no AI in it. Professional and business services contains temp help, which turns first in any slowdown, and heavy federal contracting exposure. Financial activities contains real estate and insurance, both rate-sensitive with the real 10-year at 2.4%. I cannot rule any of those out from the payload — I have no federal-contracting series and no sub-industry cut.

But the contemporaneous test for a general-macro explanation runs the other way and I should state it plainly, since it cuts *toward* an AI-specific story and therefore against my own verdict's comfort: **construction is the most interest-rate-sensitive industry in the economy and it sits in the control leg, which is growing at 1.16%.** If the exposed decline were a rate story, construction should be the first casualty and it is not. Leisure and hospitality, the most discretionary-spending-sensitive control component, is also inside a growing leg. So the weakness is specific to AI-exposed work rather than general. That is what this panel is for and it establishes it. It does not establish that anyone was displaced, and the mechanics in its measurement_artifact are decisive: if AI eliminated 100 jobs in information and all 100 of those people were hired in health care, this panel would print its maximally negative reading with every worker landing somewhere. So the reading goes to the reabsorption panel, per the binding weighting rule.

CES revision risk applies to the newest two months. Both the exposed and control legs are preliminary at 2026-07 and the birth-death model is known to under-count losses entering a downturn. That risk points against my verdict, not for it: if anything the exposed leg may be worse than printed.

*reabsorption (REABSORPTION, headline as_of 2026-07; JOLTS components 2026-06).* The headline binds and the headline is **flat: 12-month change 0.0, level 80.4, which is 0.45 points above its 2019 reference**. Deviation 0.8σ toward displacement against the clean baseline — below the attention line of 1, and both baselines agree so this does not depend on window choice. The panel's own deterioration rule is the 12-month change reaching 1σ below its 2010s norm, i.e. about −0.10; we are at 0.0, above it.

Applying the attribution panel's weighting rule literally: is the gap widening while prime-age employment, long-term unemployment and hiring hold steady? Prime-age employment 12-month change 0.0 — steady. Long-term unemployed share 25.5%, up 0.6 over twelve months, 0.31σ — mildly worse, well inside normal. Hires-minus-quits 1.4, up 0.1 over twelve months, deviation −0.9 (*away* from displacement) — steady to improving. All three hold. The rule's conclusion is that workers are moving rather than being removed, and I accept it because the underlying logic is sound, not because it is written down: a worker who left information services and was hired in health care is invisible to the exposed/control gap and visible here, and here nothing has gone missing.

The layoffs readout matters more than its weight suggests. Layoffs rate 1.1, down 0.1 over twelve months, deviation −0.34 against the clean baseline, and the 3-month horizon also falling at −0.94. Paired with hiring per the panel's own pairing rule: hires 3.4 and quits 2.0 are both low by pre-pandemic standards, layoffs are at or below norm. That is a **frozen** market, not a shedding one. Firms are not pushing out incumbents; they are not taking on entrants. This is genuinely double-edged and I will come back to it in the inversion.

Two readouts point the other way and I am not going to bury them. The **U6−U3 underemployment gap is 3.8, up 0.2 over twelve months, 1.81σ toward displacement against the clean baseline** — past the attention line. That is the "landing badly" measure, and it is the single most displacement-shaped number in the reabsorption panel. And the headline's own **3-month change is −0.3, at 1.95σ, essentially at the alarm line**, disagreeing with the 12-month figure. Both are context by the panel's construction and I am citing the 12-month horizon as the one that places the axis. But the reason those are context is not arbitrary: a 3-month change on a monthly household series is noisy and is not seasonally comparable to the 12-month figure. I note it as a hypothesis about a possible turn, which is precisely what my overturn condition is built to catch.

One population discipline point: everything in this panel is economy-wide. That is by design here — the whole question is whether the *aggregate* labour market absorbed an outflow, and only an aggregate can answer it, since neither survey follows a person from an exposed industry into a control one. But it has a hard limit I must state: I cannot say the specific people who left information and professional services are the ones now employed. I can only say the aggregate did not shed them, long-term unemployment did not spike, and layoffs did not rise. That is weaker than "they landed," and I will not overstate it.

The decomposition note is internally consistent once read carefully: employed −779k and population −937k over twelve months look alarming, but both legs cross the January control re-basing (+1.7m at Jan 2025, −1.0m at Jan 2026 on the employment leg) while the ratio does not. The published ratio is the reliable measure and it is flat. I am not quoting the level magnitudes. I also note explicitly that this figure must not be set beside the news package's −23k payroll print: household vs establishment survey, 25-54 vs all ages, twelve months vs one month. Three things differ at once and netting them would be nonsense.

*exposed_vs_control_wages (ATTRIBUTION, as_of 2026-07).* Naming the sides: **exposed pay +4.22% y/y, control +3.21%, differential +1.00**, up from 0.93 last month. Deviation −0.60, i.e. *away* from displacement, both baselines agreeing. Twenty-four consecutive months inside its own 2010s range. Taken at face value, pay in AI-exposed industries is accelerating relative to everywhere else, which is what you would expect if AI were making exposed workers more productive and employers were bidding for them.

I cannot take it at face value. The panel's weighting rule turns on the sign of exposed employment, and exposed employment is **falling** at −1.19%. When employment in a group is falling, a genuine pay story and a composition story predict the identical observation: if entry-level hiring in information, professional services and finance has stopped, the remaining workforce skews senior and the average rises with nobody receiving a raise. The juniors left the denominator. And a frozen market — which is exactly what the layoffs/hires pairing above says we are in — is the precise condition under which that artifact is largest.

The composition cross-check, individual_wage_growth, does not resolve it. Stayers 3.6%, switchers 4.4%, premium 0.8, deviation −0.54 away from displacement, recovering over the last four readings, premium above its 2010s mean of 0.58. That says the economy-wide individual-level picture is *not* flat or falling, so the aggregate acceleration is not obviously pure artifact. But it is economy-wide and cannot be cut to exposed versus control, so it cannot confirm an exposed-industry story. The honest position is that **the composition question on this panel is unresolved**, and I am weighting it accordingly — as a thin positive strand, not as proof of augmentation. Also worth noting for the "landing well" test: a switcher premium of 0.8 above its 2010s norm means people who move jobs are, at the median, landing well rather than taking pay cuts. But it is a median, so it says nothing about the tail — and the U6−U3 widening is precisely a tail measurement. Those two are not in contradiction; they are measuring different parts of the same distribution, and the median looks fine while the tail is deteriorating slightly. Vintage 2026-06 on the tracker vs 2026-07 on the wage panel and CPS is missing October 2025 entirely, so moves of a couple of tenths here are noise.

*job_postings_spread (ATTRIBUTION, as_of 2026-08, freshest panel on the board).* Naming the sides rather than the spread, as required: **knowledge-work postings sit at 76, i.e. 24% below their own February 2020 level; hands-on postings sit at 104.7, 4.7% above theirs.** The spread is −28.7. Its measurement_artifact is emphatic that the level is substantially a 2022 event still sitting there, opened before current AI tools diffused into hiring decisions and timed to the tightening cycle, so I read the change: **spread_change_over_6_months is +2.9, i.e. narrowing.** Month-over-month it widened 0.3, which against a 4.39 standard deviation is nothing.

This is the earliest-moving panel and it is cut by occupation rather than industry, which makes it a better exposure proxy than the jobs panel. It points mildly toward improvement. That matters for the third confidence doubt — the leading indicator is not pointing against my verdict. But I have a real limitation here and I will not paper over it: **I have the current levels of both sides but not their levels six months ago, so I cannot say whether the spread narrowed because exposed postings recovered or because control postings fell.** Those are opposite stories and the panel as delivered does not let me distinguish them. That alone caps how much weight this can carry. There is no fixed pre-2020 baseline (the series starts 2020-02), so no deviation figure against a clean window exists; the −1.07 against full history is computed off a window that is entirely the period under test and I discount it accordingly. Its threshold was deleted 2026-07-29; I treat that as neither reassurance nor alarm.

*labor_productivity (GAINS_TEST, economy-wide, as_of 2026-06).* 2.2%, down from 2.9%, below the 2.7 lower line for one quarter. It is 0.83σ above the 2010s mean of 1.27 — better than the 2010s but decelerating and short of the internet-boom band the threshold defines. **This does not corroborate augmentation.** If AI were delivering the productivity gains the augmentation story requires, this is where it would show, and it is going the wrong way this quarter. I record that as a strike against my own verdict's positive-evidence leg. It is economy-wide, so it can never attribute anything to AI-exposed work in either direction, and one quarter below a band after several years of solid readings is not a break. It is also the most heavily revised series here.

*worker_share_of_income (DESCRIPTIVE, economy-wide, as_of 2026-03 — five months old, more than a quarter older than my load-bearing panels, so I flag the gap).* 51.0%, four consecutive quarterly declines, −0.96 over one year against a forty-year drift of −0.13/year — roughly seven times the secular pace — and in the fastest 10% of four-quarter declines this series has produced since 1947. The level is below the previous full-history low of 51.19. This is a genuine finding and I will not leave it out just because the panel does not vote: labour's claim on national income is falling fast, to a record, *outside* a recession, with unemployment at 4.1%. The panel's own note is that ordinary recessions produced faster falls (−2.18 in 2009, −1.59 in 2010) so any threshold here would fire on recessions — but the point cuts the other way at the moment, because we are not in a recession and this is still moving at recessionary speed. What it cannot do is attribute: it is economy-wide, GDI-based and heavily revised, it has fallen since the 1970s for causes that predate AI by decades, and nothing connects its movement to AI-exposed work. It raises my unease about the augmentation reading; it does not move the verdict, and its five-month vintage means it cannot reflect anything since March.

*ai_adoption (DEPLOYMENT_CONTEXT, as_of 2026-07).* 21.5% of firms, up from 17.3% in nine months, rising in seven of eight months. Size gradient 1.77x: 36.8% at firms with 250+ employees against 20.8% at the smallest, which means the share of *workers* at an AI-using employer is materially higher than 21.5% — though no employment-weighted figure is measured and I will not invent one. The genuine finding: diffusion is real and steadily rising, so the objection "it's too early for AI to be doing anything" is getting weaker every month. What this cannot do is supply a reason. The survey asks whether a tool is *present in any business function*, not whether any use case made a role redundant — which is the thing that would actually cost a job. And it is an economy-wide aggregate with no firm-level linkage: nothing here connects any given company's adoption to that same company's hiring freeze, so pairing this series with any employment series compares two aggregates and tells you nothing about mechanism. A self-reported "yes" can be one pilot nobody uses, from a firm that likes sounding forward-leaning. It removes an objection; it does not carry evidence.

*ai_use_automation_vs_augmentation.* 56.9% augmentation, 43.1% automation, stable across three releases. Eleven months stale, measuring the fastest-moving thing here, over one vendor's conversation sample where a shift in *who is using the product* moves the split with nobody changing how they work. Conversations are not jobs. I note only that the split was stable across the releases that exist; it predates every labour month on this board by most of a year and I give it no weight in a current call — it would be embarrassing to lean on a September 2025 reading to describe August 2026.

*macro_regime (CONFOUNDER_CHECK, as_of 2026-08).* Curve not inverted (10y−2y +0.5), real 10-year 2.4%, expected inflation 2.3%. This can name a cyclical hypothesis and it cannot clear one, because it prices what investors expect rather than what already happened. So I ran the contemporaneous test on the control panels instead, and reported it above: construction, the most rate-sensitive industry in the economy, sits in a control leg growing at 1.16%. The rate hypothesis does not survive that. A real 10-year at 2.4% is restrictive enough to plausibly weigh on real estate and insurance inside the exposed leg, which is a partial confounder on the exposed side I cannot quantify from this payload — but it cannot be the whole story while construction is fine.

*Capability panels (METR, GDPval ratings, GDPval vs experts).* Read, counted in nothing. METR's frontier is at 186 minutes at the 80% reliability level, against a 40-hour reference bar that sits about 2.5x beyond what the task suite can score reliably — so the projected 2027-10 crossing is a marker on a forecast rather than an event anyone will observe, and I would not quote it. The GDPval-vs-experts series is the most persuasive-looking of the three because there is a human on the other side, and it is worth noting that at 70.9% wins-plus-ties the true parity figure is 49.7% wins-only, that the top figure is OpenAI reporting on OpenAI's benchmark, and that nothing has been published since December 2025. But none of this is labor evidence in either direction: clearing an expert on a scored task and an employer deciding to stop paying that expert are different events, separated by however long deployment takes, and no series here links them. The Elo move of +2.6 that showed up in "what changed" tells me which lab is ahead this month and nothing about anyone's employment.

---

**Inversions — the strongest opposite reading of each panel I am leaning on.**

*Inverting reabsorption.* This is the best version of the displacement case and it is not weak. A flat prime-age employment share is exactly what a frozen labour market produces when displacement operates through hiring freezes and attrition rather than layoffs. Prime-age EPOP is dominated by people who already have jobs; if firms simply stop replacing leavers and stop hiring entrants, incumbents keep working, the ratio holds, and the damage falls entirely on people trying to enter — who are disproportionately young and therefore under-weighted even in the 25-54 cut. The panel's own pairing rule says weak hiring plus at-or-below-norm layoffs *is* a frozen market, and hires at 3.4 and quits at 2.0 are both low. Under this reading, my "absorption is holding" finding is really "incumbents have not been fired yet," which is a much smaller claim. And the two readouts that would show the early edge of removal both point that way: U6−U3 at 1.81σ says a growing share of people are landing part-time-for-economic-reasons or dropping out of the count, and the headline's own 3-month change at −0.3 sits at 1.95σ, essentially the alarm line, disagreeing with the 12-month figure I am citing. Twelve-month changes are lagging by construction. If the turn began in the second quarter, the 12-month change is the last place it would appear. **I am aware I am citing the slower horizon and that the faster one disagrees.** My reasons for still citing it: a 3-month change on a monthly household series is noisy and not seasonally comparable to the 12-month figure, and it is contradicted within the same panel by JOLTS layoffs falling on both horizons and by a genuinely different survey. But this is the doubt that would flip me, which is why my overturn condition is built on exactly this field.

*Inverting exposed_vs_control_wages.* The opposite reading is close to the panel's default: exposed pay running 1.0 point ahead of control while exposed employment falls 1.19% is the signature of the juniors leaving the denominator. On that reading this panel is not evidence against displacement at all — it is a symptom of displacement concentrated at the entry level, where the average rises precisely *because* the cheap workers were the ones who went. The individual-level tracker cannot rebut this, because it is economy-wide and cannot be cut to exposed industries; a healthy economy-wide switcher premium is fully consistent with exposed-industry entrants being frozen out while everyone else does fine. I accept this: the composition question is unresolved and I am reporting the panel as weak support rather than at face value. It is the reason my confidence is LOW rather than MEDIUM.

*Inverting job_postings_spread.* Two opposite readings, both real. First, the level: exposed knowledge-work postings have sat roughly a quarter below their own pre-pandemic baseline for four years while hands-on postings sit above theirs. That is a structurally impaired demand picture for exactly the work AI touches, and a 2.9-point narrowing off a −31.6 base leaves it essentially where it has been. Second, and worse for me: since I do not have the six-month-ago levels of each side, the narrowing could be the *control* side weakening toward the exposed side rather than the exposed side recovering — which would be a general deterioration, not an exposed-side improvement. I cannot exclude that from this payload, and it is a serious limitation on a panel I am citing as support. Also worth stating flatly: hands-on postings being strong is a fact about hands-on work and is not evidence of augmentation in knowledge work. A knowledge worker who ends up in a hands-on role has not been augmented.

*Inverting the reabsorption layoffs readout specifically.* Layoffs at 1.1 and falling is economy-wide. Exposed-industry layoffs could be elevated while the aggregate is calm, because information plus professional plus financial services is a minority of total employment and a large control-side sector can mask it. There is no exposed-industry cut of JOLTS on this board, so I cannot check this. It is a genuine hole in my case.

---

**Rejected hypotheses.**

*CONFOUNDED on interest rates.* Named cause: restrictive real rates (macro_regime, real 10-year 2.4%) hitting rate-sensitive financial activities inside the exposed leg and rate-sensitive white-collar postings, with the postings artifact explicitly attributing the 2022 opening of that spread to the tightening cycle. Rejected as the verdict, because the contemporaneous test fails it: construction, the single most rate-sensitive industry in the economy, is in the control leg, which is growing at 1.16%. A rate story that spares construction while killing information-sector employment is not a rate story. It remains a partial confounder on the financial-activities component of the exposed leg, which I cannot size.

*CONFOUNDED on federal contracting.* Professional and business services carries heavy federal contracting exposure, and a contraction there would register as AI-exposed job loss with no AI in it. I have no series in the payload showing federal contracting volumes or federal employment, and CONFOUNDED requires a named cause *plus* the series that supports it. Named without a series is speculation, so it does not qualify.

*CONFOUNDED on media strikes / sector consolidation.* The 2023 peak in this differential coincides with the writers' and actors' strikes, which is a live warning about this industry code. But that was three years ago and nothing in the payload or news package indicates a current work stoppage. Rejected for lack of a current supporting series.

*"Mixed evidence" as grounds for CONFOUNDED.* It is not, and this reading is mixed. It goes out as a directional call with the weakness in the rating.

---

**News package.**

*BLS Employment Situation, through 2026-07: nonfarm payrolls 158,858k, −23k on the month; unemployment 4.1%.* A negative payroll print is the most consequential item here and it generates a real hypothesis: the aggregate labour market may be turning, in which case my "absorption holding" reading is about to expire. Tested against the series: it is one month, economy-wide, all ages, from the establishment survey whose two most recent months are preliminary and whose birth-death model is known to miss turning points entering a downturn. The household survey's prime-age employment share, which is the binding headline here and runs to the same month, is flat over twelve months. I am explicitly not netting −23k against the −779k in the CPS decomposition; those differ in survey, age range and horizon simultaneously, and the payload warns against it. Unemployment at 4.1% is not a distressed labour market. Verdict unmoved, but this is precisely the kind of thing my overturn condition is designed to catch if it persists for three more prints.

*AP wire: Iran war, inflation, mortgage rates, Fed.* A war could move energy prices and hiring. I looked for a mechanism that would produce *this* pattern — information, professional and financial employment contracting while construction, leisure/hospitality and education/health grow — and could not construct one. An energy and confidence shock hits discretionary leisure spending and construction materials costs at least as hard as it hits software and consulting; it would compress the exposed-control gap, not open it. It is also too recent to be inside July payroll data. The mortgage/Fed thread is the rate hypothesis handled above and it fails on construction. Set aside on mechanism, not on vintage alone.

*NY Fed Liberty Street, "AI's Impact on Labor and Hiring," August 2026.* An institutional piece whose findings are not in my payload, so I cannot cite conclusions I do not have. What it does is generate the obvious hypothesis: AI is suppressing hiring in exposed work. I tested that direction against the series rather than treating it as corroboration — and it partly survives (exposed employment negative, layoffs low, which is the signature of a freeze rather than a purge) and partly fails (the aggregate did not shed people, long-term unemployment barely moved, hiring against quitting improved). On attribution incentives: any employer testimony in such coverage runs both ways — attributing headcount to AI reads as forward-leaning to investors, while attributing it to AI attracts political and regulatory attention that "macro headwinds" does not. So a quote in either direction is a hypothesis, and I tested the pro-AI direction against the reabsorption panel specifically, where it did not produce removal. News never moves the verdict; the series did.

---

**Vintage discipline.** Load-bearing panels: job_postings_spread 2026-08 (0 months), reabsorption headline 2026-07 (1 month, with its JOLTS components at 2026-06), exposed_vs_control_wages 2026-07 (1 month). All within one quarter of each other; the JOLTS lag means a very recent turn would appear in the household headline before hires/quits/layoffs caught up, which is worth holding. The evidence arguing *against* my verdict is not older than the evidence supporting it — exposed_vs_control_jobs and U6−U3 are both 2026-07, i.e. fresher than the individual wage tracker (2026-06) and the productivity panel (2026-06) that I am partly leaning on. So the counterweight is fully capable of reflecting a recent turn, and it does not yet show removal. worker_share_of_income at 2026-03 is five months old, more than a quarter behind the postings panel; I stated the gap where I discussed it and did not lean on it.

---

**Confidence reasoning, against the three doubts.**

*Does the signal persist or rest on the last reading or two?* The calm side persists: prime-age employment has been at or near flat for a year, layoffs have been low throughout, and the exposed/control divergence has been present since 2023 while *shrinking* from 5.66σ to 1.82σ. So my reading is not a one-print artifact.
